en: [Oṃ, salutation to the Guru who is the letter *kāra*. Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ arhaṃ, salutation to Gautamasvāmin.
[Salutation be to the Blessed Śramaṇa Mahāvīra.
[Composed by the Sage Śrī Dhanēśvara.]
[Surasundarīcaritra] [p.
1] Of him who has undertaken worldly duties at the proper time, according to the vows and observances of a lay follower.
The mass of his hair, held by the command of the Queen of the Immortals, is exceedingly curly;
it shines near his ear as if it were the god Kandarpa himself, whose entry was blocked within his heart and who remained there for the sake of seeking a place to stay. (SurSūCa.1–2)
Or rather:
He shines, whose beautiful, well-arranged mass of hair trembles upon both shoulders;
his complexion is golden-hued, like the flame of a lamp with soot upon its tip.
I bow with devotion to the first lotus-feet of that Ṛṣabha, at whose prostration even a multitude of obstacles, though vast, meets its destruction. (SurSūCa.4)
[I praise the four groups in a quatrain: I bow to the Lord of Jinas, Ajitājin, in whose life even the enemies—passion and the rest—met their destruction along with Māra. (SurSūCa. 5)
At the moment immediately following his birth, during the time of his consecration on the peak of Mount Meru, when the seat of the thunderbolt was fashioned by Śakra and Indra, he exerted himself;
for even the enemy of passion (Rāga) found it impossible to behold his peerless power. (SurSūCa. 6)
The earth, with its mountains and oceans, trembled violently;
the rays of whose stainless teeth reflected the three worlds of devotees and bore the pride of being the equal of absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*). (SurSūCa 7–8)
And at whose mere salutation, the gods— seeing their own reflections in his stainless eye-like nails and perceiving themselves as possessing eleven qualities— were filled with joy.
(SurSūCa.9)

I pay homage to that Jina-Indra, who is worshipped by hosts of lords of gods and lords of men, the son of King Siddhārtha, who has attained the final, ultimate state of liberation. (SurSūCa 10) [A group of five verses].
I bow my head in homage to the Siddha, who is like a preeminent lion among the deer that are the deceptive limbs of the unconquerable god of love, and who dwells with the eternal bliss of liberation.
(SurSūCa.11) To the steadfast one, who teaches the firm and established doctrine that utterly destroys the teeth of evil [opponents]...

With my head bowed, I revere the Ācāryas who delight in the five modes of conduct (pañcavihāyāra). I constantly revere the Upādhyāyas, who are free from thirst for the pleasures of the senses and are intent upon severing the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), being experts in the meaning of the scriptures.
I bow my head in homage to all the sages who have abandoned the bonds of household life and are capable of scaling the mountains of the five great vows and the two-fold self-restraint;
by obtaining whose lotus-feet, living beings attain the supreme state.
Victorious is the Goddess Sarasvatī, who possesses knowledge even through ignorance;
and by her grace, I too, though dull-witted, have engaged in the composition of this narrative.

Līlā is set in motion; especially, I bow to those teachers. (SurSūCa.16) Thus, having dispelled the entire multitude of obstacles by performing prostrations to the worshipful ones, I shall speak the discourse named *Surasundarī*, which inspires a sense of renunciation. (SurSūCa.17)

Food is offered first of all to that wicked person from whom the poet flees like a mouse from a cat; or rather, it is simply his nature, for his mind is ever occupied with finding faults. (SurSūCa.18)
Even through repeated entreaties, the wickedness of a wicked person does not fade away.
A double-tongued person, seeking to test others and remaining crooked even when solicited by poets, is like a snake. (SurSūCa.19–20)
Even when inwardly composed, the wicked man— crooked, with a defiled heart, and devoid of good conduct— reveals his attachment to faults here like the moon.
(SurSūCa.21)
Whether in a poem that is charming or harsh, a fault must be perceived by the wicked;
or rather, like a lizard from its hole, it never emerges.
Even a flawless poem, having fallen into the company of the wicked, finds no firm footing.
Like a drop of water cast into a vessel of heated iron, (the praise of) a poet who has encountered a wicked person is indeed in vain;
for even when drenched with the juice of sugar, the neem tree does not abandon its bitterness. (SurSūCa.23–24)
Or rather, why should a composition of stories be withheld out of fear of wicked people?
Indeed, it is not right to abandon gambling for fear of a loss.
Even if it is disapproved of by the wicked, what is improper here in a poet’s work?
Does not the sun rise even when not speaking of its own greatness? Even though he is not sought after, the good man reveals virtues in the poetry of poets;
by his very nature, the moon whitens the entire world. (SurSūCa 26–27)
A virtuous person never seizes upon the faults of even those who revile them; even while being carved, a sandalwood tree does not become fragrant with the scent of the axe. (SurSūCa.28)
Even food becomes delicious through association with good people, and even a poem becomes excellent;
even water placed inside a pearl-oyster shell becomes a pearl. (SurSūCa.
29) Since good people are worthy of being entreated, we now request them.
Listen with one-pointed minds as it is being explained:
having obtained the human state—which is extremely difficult for a worldly being to attain—in this terrible, shoreless cycle of existence filled with hundreds of thousands of wombs. (SurSūCa 30–31)
The Jinas, who are worshipped by the lords of gods, the lords of serpents, the lords of the wind-gods, and the lords of men, have proclaimed: "It is fitting to exert oneself in the pure Dharma.
For that [Dharma] conquers the internal enemy, as well as diseases and faults, which are the internal foes.
In their victory alone lies the happiness of living beings, and through them comes suffering once more.
Such being the case, living beings, overcome by passion and hatred, undergo various kinds of suffering. (SurSūCa.33) [p. 7]
Therefore, the wise should strive for that very conquest [of the self].
(SurSūCa 34) This story, named *Surasundarī*, composed in elegant Prakrit verses, is devoted to the accomplishment of this goal and is comprised of sixteen chapters. (SurSūCa 35)
It is not possible for poets to simultaneously accomplish both the instruction of ignorant people and the delighting of the minds of those who find pleasure in difficult compositions;
for the learned person is delighted by that which is adorned with poetic figures and composed of dense syllables. (SurSūCa. 36)
It reveals poetry that is charming in its subject matter and brings enlightenment even to the unlearned. (SurSūCa.
37) It is possible to please both [parties] only by remaining neutral;
for those who take one side, the second will surely be lost. (SurSūCa. 38)
Even if I possess some slight capacity for poetry abounding in similes, metaphors, forms, and descriptions, it is nonetheless weighted down by a lack of self-confidence. (SurSūCa.
Nevertheless, even when one is incapable regarding the desired object, that [instruction] is not performed;
therefore, this [instruction] is made explicit for the sake of awakening the unintelligent.
Furthermore, [this was said] because the sister of the Guru, who was the mother of Śiṣyinī, had not received the oral instruction.
At the request of the female teacher Śrī Kalyāṇamati, this [work] was begun;
because of my pride in poetic composition (*kavitta*), I have not composed it with Prakrit verses of elegant phrasing. (SurSūCa 41–42)

Enough with this excessive, futile, and obstructive talk, which is like the sidelong glances cast by a girl from a wealthy family! Now listen with one-pointed minds as this story is being told. (SurSūCa. 43)
This [work] consists of two hundred and fifty verses, having been composed as a summary.
Herein, there is a very extensive description of the middle region of the upward world, namely the horizontal world (tiryagloka), which is frequented by the wise and resembles Mount Sumeru.
There is also an island there, extending for a hundred thousand yojanas, known as Jambūdvīpa, which is surrounded by a ring of ocean. (SurSūCa.46)

To its southern side there is a magnificent region named Bharata, which is divided into two parts by the Vaitāḍhya mountain range and is very extensive. Now, in southern half-Bharata, in the middle between the Gaṅgā and Sindhu rivers...
Like the wish-fulfilling tree among trees, he was the preeminent benefactor of many lands;

his ears were filled with the clamor of crowds of prosperous and flourishing peasants, and his territory was inhabited by various domestic animals such as sheep, goats, buffaloes, bulls, and oxen. (SurSūCa 48–49)
Its gardens were shimmering with the flow of canals that carried away the dust raised by the hooves of horses;

it was filled with cities, towns, villages, and ports, and all its people were enriched with great prosperity. Its inhabitants were constantly delighted, never lacking various kinds of festivals. (SurSūCa 50)
There was a noble land named Kuru, a village free from fear and turmoil.
[SurSuCa.51] [With four verses, a *kalāpaka*] [p. 10]

Furthermore, in that region—a dwelling place for entire armies of merchants whose caravans were incessantly driven by robbers—it was impossible to distinguish, at every step, the specific locations within the forest. Moreover, in that land, which was a treasury of virtues, this was a marvel:

SurSuCa.52: Furthermore, in that region—a dwelling place for entire armies of merchants whose caravans were incessantly driven by robbers—it was impossible to distinguish, at every step, the specific locations within the forest.
Moreover, in that land, which was a treasury of virtues, this was a marvel:
Even the common folk hear the worldly sayings proclaimed by the scribes.
Furthermore, who would take the effort to praise that country where the village elders are exempt from taxes and devoid of righteousness? (SurSūCa 53–54)
And there too, it was surrounded by a moat resembling the vast circle of the ocean,
impassable for enemy men, and filled with swarming crocodiles; it was encompassed by a beautiful,
expansive wall that inspired fear in adversaries.
It was surrounded by beautiful gateways with arched doorways;
its outer sections were adorned with very dark and thick groves of trees, and it was endowed with excellent,
variegated balconies and windows.
[11] It is eternally delightful with palaces joined by various floors, white as snow, which resemble the masses of fame of the inhabitants of that city. (SurSūCa. 58)

It was resplendent with numerous market-stalls where trade was being conducted day after day by the merchant community— both those who had arrived from various distant lands and those residing in that very city—
who were skilled in the arts of commerce.

Its beautiful areas were adorned with well-constructed temples of the gods, filled within with highly precious jewels, and featuring lofty Makara-archways where white banners fluttered in the wind. (SurSūCa 60–61)

Likewise, it was adorned with twenty thousand staircases that were easy to traverse, which were like swarms of bees beautifying a cluster of white lotuses; and it was graced with excellent triple-gateways,
quadrangles, crossroads, groves, gardens, and lotus ponds.
Even for the gods, he causes the withdrawal of their minds at every step; [he went to] the city named Śrī-Āḍhasthināpura, the preeminent among all cities and kingdoms. (SurSūCa.63) [p. 12]

It was as beautiful as the city of the gods, possessing the virtues of right conduct; there the people dwelt, speaking kindly and being intensely devoted to the practice of Dharma. (SurSūCa.64) [A group of ten verses] Where the people reside, they are pleasant-spoken and ever-desirous of performing righteous deeds.

In that city, which was difficult to traverse due to crowds of people constantly moving here and there, intent on many activities such as giving alms, receiving gifts, and enjoying pleasures, he was likewise skilled in the arts. (SurSūCa 65–66)

In that city, where the entire path of the sky was concealed by banners reaching a distance of ten million [yojanas], the people did not even perceive the heat of the sun’s rays during the summer days. And in that city, men [were illuminated] by the radiance of jewels placed within the walls of their houses.
Even when it is perpetually shrouded in darkness, they do not perceive even the night.
Because of its beauty, the gods have come as if for the sake of gazing upon it; their minds captivated by curiosity, they have attained a state of unblinking eyes.
With victory banners fluttering in the wind atop their white turrets, the [palaces] seem to stand as if to support the charioteer of the sun as he ascends too high. (SurSūCa. 70)

And in that city, where a kick with the foot is seen on the stages, a staff is used for banners, and the cutting off of heads belongs to wrestlers; where flowers are bound upon the head, there is the role of a physician only at funerals. (SurSuCa.71)
Thus, alas! there is the breaking [of the pots] for those who have arrived at the assemblies of the wise.
But indeed, there is only one fault in that city which is the abode of virtues:
that faultless monks are seen there constantly, established in self-restraint.
Now, in that city, there was a lord who possessed abundant treasures of elephants, horses, and jewels;

whose heart was gladdened by hundreds of subjects through the observance of the dharma as it had been proclaimed; and who, by the ocean of his own intellect, had brought under his control the entire lineage of his enemies. (SurSūCa. 74)
He has fulfilled the ocean of goals desired by his mind,
and he has overcome all adversaries through his firm resolve and arms and his immeasurable prowess.
He whose mind causes the lotus-faces of his adversaries to close like the moon;

he who possesses vast majesty like the sun; who, like a lion, has no fear of the enemy forces; who is as profoundly deep as the ocean; and who, like the moon, brings joy to the hearts of the people. (SurSūCa.76–77)
In beauty like the God of Love and in intellect equal to the Preceptor of the Gods, King Śrī Amarakeu dwells having attained great joy. (SurSūCa.
78) [A group of five verses].
As he was duly enjoying the glory of his kingdom, which had the three groups as its essence,
the days passed like those of Indra in the world of the gods. Then, on a certain occasion, while that king was seated in the assembly hall—
The gatekeeper Bandhula, whose head was bowed in humility, said:
"O Lord, a painter named Citrasena, who has arrived from Kusagrapura with a canvas for his work, is standing at the gate. (SurSūCa. 80–81)
“Desiring the happiness of seeing the Lord, he wishes for entry here;
and since this is the case, ‘The command of our Lord is authoritative’—thus [he spoke]. (SurSūCa.82)

Then the king said, "Bring him in quickly. Thereupon, he entered the assembly hall according to the prescribed ritual and, having performed a salutation before the king, sat down upon the ground. The king asked him, "From where have you come, O blessed one?"
"For what purpose have you come here into my presence? [The king asked. Then Citrasena replied: "O Lord, I have come from the city of Kusāgra;
I am a painter and I know the extraordinary art of painting. (SurSūCa.84–85)

"And it is heard that you are a god skilled in painting; therefore, I have come here into the presence of the king to manifest my artistic skill. Then the king said, "What kind of proficiency in painting do you possess?"
"First, O Daṃsa, you have painted some beautiful form upon me; then, suddenly, that picture-cloth was hidden by him in the region of my armpit. (SurSūCa.87) [p. 16]
Having made it manifest, they presented it to the king with joyful words.
With his hair standing on end from manifest joy, the king gazed there upon that which was drawn, adorned with various colors, and perfectly pure in its proportions and lines. (SurSūCa 88–89)

Seeing that most enchanting form of the maiden, endowed with the excellent beauty of fresh youth and like the very commencement of a new moon, the lord of men thought: "This is indeed a work of art. (SurSūCa. 90)

"Whatever unskillful person has painted this form of such unprecedented beauty—in all the three worlds, I believe, there is no woman of such appearance; through her skill in the art of painting, she has been depicted here as one whose true form was never seen. (SurSūCa 91–92)
If, however, there should be a maiden of such a form anywhere, and if union with her were possible, then the kingdom would be truly successful. (SurSūCa.93) [p.
While he was thinking thus, having fallen into the range of the arrows of love, his own self was forgotten by him as his mind was distracted.
Then, in that very moment, Amarakeu closed his eyes. (SurSūCa. 94)
He suddenly fell from his lion-throne, overcome by fainting.
Crying out "Alas! Alas! the people gathered in the assembly hall rose up;
they fanned him with fans and sprinkled him with cool water.
They quickly threw camphor into his mouth and likewise smeared their limbs [with it] upon seeing him;
Cittasena became intensely enraged, his face breaking into a laugh:
"Hey! Hey! Some wicked person has surely come here in the form of a serpent! (SurSūCa. 97)
"By whom has he been so deluded here that he says, 'He is our master'?
While the bodyguards were saying, "Beat him! Strike him! Bind him!", they seized him; and as he was being beaten, he began to speak thus: (SurSūCa.98–99)
“O, O, noble ones! I am not wicked; therefore, do not vainly reproach me.
Then they said: “How are you not wicked, O sinner? (SurSūCa.100)
"Why did you gaze upon the king's body with such intent?
And why did your face bloom with joy even when the lord was about to die?
Therefore, tell me, O wicked one! By whom were you sent to bring about the king's death?"
Cittasena said: "I shall tell you everything.
I have come for the sake of the king's prosperity, and not with evil intent.
Even as he was speaking these words, he was bound by the king's men.
In the meantime, the king regained consciousness and his senses returned.
Then the king said: "Ho there! Release this painted house! Once its bonds were loosened by the king, he was addressed: "My good man, sit down!"
"Tell me the truth: by whom have you been sent here?
Then Citrasena said: "Listen, O Lord of Men! To the ultimate truth of the matter."
Wearing the guise of a madman, he arrived here by whom I [was brought].
Here is the well-known Kusāgrapura, possessing the virtues of a city protected by the gods, abounding in wealth and grain, and filled with people. (SurSūCa 106–107)
There lived a king named Ghanavāhana, whose ears were filled with the praises of his subjects;
he had a queen dearer to him than life, named Vasantasenā.
Their son was Naravāhana by name, possessed of intense majesty.

A daughter named Kamalāvatī, possessed of exceedingly beautiful form, [was born]. Then, on another occasion, the king thought: "Having bestowed my own kingdom upon Naravāhana, my sister Kamalāvatī must be given to a suitable husband."

Having spoken thus to his son, he, having conceived a sense of spiritual urgency, duly entered the ascetic life that severs the cycle of worldly existence in the presence of a true teacher. (SurSūCa.111) [p.
King Naravāhana also protects his kingdom, whose enemies have been subdued;
Kamalāvatī likewise dwells happily within the inner apartments of the harem. Furthermore, in that city there lived a merchant named Sāgara.
The king had a childhood friend who was deeply devoted to the words of the Jina.
His wife, named Śrīmatī, was very dear to him and endowed with virtuous conduct; his son was Śrīdatta, and likewise his daughter was Śrīkāntā. (SurSūCa.113–114)
Sirikantā went to Kamalāvatī’s side every day, and a great mutual affection arose between them both.
Even in her childhood, she had acquired the arts through association with women. (SurSūCa. 115)
In the presence of Sumitra-sena, who was skilled in all arts, Śrīkāntā would sport with the princess through various delightful pastimes,
and then return home at the time of evening.
[21] A long time passed for Śrīkāntā, the king’s daughter, who was devoted to various kinds of play and whose essence was affection. (SurSūCa.118)
Gradually increasing, their forms became desirable even to the gods; they reached the abode of the amorous adornment of the God of Love in the prime of their youth.
Then, on another occasion, the king, accompanied by Maïsāgara and Sāgara...
While he was sitting in the courtyard pavilion,
Kamalāvatī arrived there accompanied by her own circle of friends;
her limbs were adorned with ornaments as she played with a ball.
Then that sister was seated on his lap by the king out of affection;
having seen her beauty and such exalted youth, the king said to the minister Maïsāgara: "By you, when setting out..."
Then I was told: "A sister should be given in marriage; now that she has become suitable for a bridegroom, tell me about her. [SurSūCa.123] [p. 22]

"Who is a man suitable for her, born of a noble family? Maheśāgara replied, "Only Your Majesty knows what is appropriate in this matter. Then the King said, "This is what flashes in my mind. (SurSūCa.124–125)
"Let a svayaṃvara be held here; let all the kings be summoned, so that she may choose him alone who is dear to her heart.
Maheśāgara said, "Whatever Your Majesty commands must be done."
However, it is not proper to perform a *svayaṃvara* (self-choice marriage) now;
for when all the kings have been brought under the control of a single lord of men, only then, with his permission, should a *svayaṃvara* be held. (SurSūCa. 127–128)
The victory of one becomes the prevention of the rest;
but now, O King, all the monarchs are indeed like Indra.
(SurSūCa.129)
Among those, in one instance they become friends, while all the others become enemies;
moreover, it is not possible for even one person to conquer them all in battle.
Therefore, O best of men, enough with this strife which is rooted in conflict and abounds in calamity.
On this occasion, regarding the choice of Kamalāvatī’s husband, the King then said:
"Whose [daughter] is she, O blessed one? To whom should she be given? And who here is dear to her heart? How indeed is this to be known? (SurSūCa. 131–132)
"To whichever king it may belong, she must be given; my own sister has not been given away by me.
She is well-given to him to whom she belongs; to him she should be given.
While the king was speaking thus there with Matisāgara—
Then the doorkeeper, rising with a prostration, said:
"O King, a fortune-teller named Śunaka has arrived here; he is an expert in the eight signs of omens and is established in the revelation of the meaning of past and future events."
"He is now standing at the entrance for the purpose of seeing the deity"; hearing this, the king said, "Let him enter quickly. (SurSuCa.136)
Immediately thereafter, Sumati, his body adorned with pure white garments,
having applied yellow orpiment as a tilaka mark, arrived before the king.
After first offering him a seat, he gave [the following] advice to the lord of men.

Having been honored by the king, he sat upon a suitable seat. When questioned by the king regarding past events for the sake of verification, he related everything truly and accurately, as if it were before his very eyes. (SurSūCa.138–139)
With a smiling face, King Naravāhana said this to him:
"O Sumati! This girl Kamalāvatī is my sister. Tell me, who will become her husband, the one dear to her heart?"
Having observed Sumati, he spoke thus regarding the omen:
"O best of men! Having beheld her form depicted in this painting..."
"He who shall become her husband here will faint [with joy];
she shall be his great queen, preeminent over all women.
O Lord of Men! Do not harbor any other thought regarding this matter. (SurSūCa.142–143)
In the meantime, the merchant Sāgara spoke to the astrologer Sumati:
"O Sirikantā, who will be the husband of my daughter? Then Sumati replied:
"She has been bitten by a black serpent; whoever [drinks] this..."
"He alone shall restore life; he will become the husband of your daughter.
(SurSūCa.145) Having thus questioned him and performed the appropriate hospitality for him, the king sent Sumati back the way he had come. (SurSūCa.146)
Then the minister said: "O King, now that this auspicious opportunity has arisen, you must now exert yourself in accordance with what he has said.
(SurSuCa.147) [p. 26]
The king asked, "Who here paints such extraordinary murals?
Maṇisāgara replied, "In this city,
there is one person who is well-known as the teacher of Kamalāvatī, named Sumitra Sena."
Then Citrasena, who was highly skilled in the art of painting, was summoned by the king;
"Summon him quickly," he said, and at that very moment, I did so.

Vāharī arrived and was addressed with great honor by the king: "Quickly paint Kamalāvatī’s form upon a picture-board, exactly as you are commanded. Having said this, he painted it with beautiful colors.
Having shown it to the king and seen his extraordinary power,
the king was pleased and said to me, "In this matter, you have acted rightly. Then, assuming the guise of a painter, I took this [painting] before all the kings.
"Whosoever feels attachment upon seeing this wonder, he must come quickly to me so that I may deal with him accordingly.
(SurSūCa.153) [p.
27] Thus spoke the Lord.
"Out of great favor, this Kamalāvatī is being given [to you].
Having been addressed thus by the king, he then bowed at his lotus-feet.
Accompanied by a few attendants, he departed from the city of Kusagga.
(SurSūCa.155) This [instruction] was shown to me by kings such as Suggīva and Kittivaddhana, yet here no success in my purpose has been achieved. (SurSūCa.156)
"O Lord! Having arrived here in this city today and having seen this [man] in your presence, fainting occurred for you. O King!
Thinking, 'The desire of my master has been fulfilled,' by him—" (SurSūCa.157)
"Joy has arisen within me upon remembering the words of the astrologer.
For this reason, O King, I am delighted by your fainting fit; do not therefore entertain any other thought regarding me. (SurSūCa.158–159)
[28] Having heard the words of Citta’s army, Amaraketu, freed from fear and wonder-struck by Citta’s form, spoke. (SurSūCa. 160)
"What kind of beauty and grace does that maiden possess?
Citrasena replied, "This was painted by me in a mere moment;
for who, even if highly skilled, is able to depict that royal maiden exactly as she truly is? (SurSūCa. 161)

"How could one paint a form that has conquered the beauty of all the playful celestial nymphs? Having heard those words, the king, with a heart filled with joy, bestowed upon him all his personal ornaments, garments, and jewelry.
Cittasena said:
"O Lord, grant us an audience so that we may report to King Naravāhana exactly as it happened.
Permitted by the king, he arrived in due course at the city of Kusāgrapura.
The entire account was reported to King Naravāhaṇa.
Then,
she too [was brought], accompanied by her own sister and a great retinue of wealth and attendants.
Below the earth, after addressing her kinsfolk, headed by Śrīkāntā, as well as the entire retinue of Amarakeu, Kamalāvatī set out, her heart overwhelmed with both joy and sorrow. (SurSūCa. 166–167)
Having obtained her desired boon, she was filled with joy; yet, due to the separation from her kinsmen, she was somewhat sorrowful.
Gradually, she arrived in Hastināpura. With great magnificence, at an auspicious moment, and with profound delight, she entered the city.
King Kamalāvatī was married according to the rites of the Kṣatriya clan. She became even dearer than his own life, the most excellent among the entire harem;
like Indrāṇī to Indra, she became the Great Queen (Mahādevī).
While that king was experiencing sensual pleasures together with her, he protected his entire realm according to the principles of righteous conduct. (SurSūCa.171) [p.
The days passed for him as he experienced an incomparable flood of happiness in the abode of the gods, a festival for the learned, where no suffering was seen.
And in that city, there lived a famous and eminent man named Dhanadharma, who was well-versed in the ancient lore.
The merchant was beloved by the king and proficient in all branches of learning;

having bestowed excellent gifts that surpassed the extensive wealth sought by everyone without exception, he was adorned with prosperity acquired through his ancestors, grandfathers, fathers, and mothers.

Expert in the extensive treatises of the Jina’s doctrine, longing for the path to liberation, devoted to the worship of the Jina’s ascetics, and exceedingly compassionate toward his fellow monks; surpassing the excellence of the beauty of celestial nymphs, he was a lamp [of wisdom] and skillful. (SurSūCa 175)

He had a wife named Manoramā, who was very dear to him as his own life. While they were fully enjoying the pleasures of the senses— the essence of the three aims of life— a single son, the ornament of their own family, was born to them.
And when twelve days had passed, his parents, according to the custom of their own family,
properly bestowed upon him the name Dhanadeva. (SurSūCa.178)

Then, that son, who was cherished with manifold delights in five ways, grew up and reached the state of youth, bringing joy to his mother and father. When he was slightly over eight years old, having properly mastered all branches of knowledge— *SurSūCa.179*.

Though he was well-born and possessed of the full range of learned arts, in a very short time he mastered all the sciences and the entire collection of arts; thus he too became one who had attained his goal. (SurSūCa 180–181)
Then, having mastered the arts, Dhanadeva was brought home by his father; the teacher was honored by him with garments and other gifts.
Gradually growing up, Dhanadeva attained youth.
Having conquered the form of the god of love, he became the husband of excellent women.

lies the city of Camaracañcā, adorned with groves of all kinds of trees.
There, moreover, was a lord of the Vidyādharas named Bhānugati, of incomparable power,
whose beauty had conquered that of the God of Love, and who brought joy to the hearts of women.
To him, the preeminent Vidyādhara Haricandra gave his own daughter, Bandhusundarī.
She was given in marriage by him with great joy and affection.
Experiencing her company with intense love, he enjoyed the kingdom, following his inclinations toward the five kinds of sense objects. (SurSūCa 33–34)
As those days passed for that queen, a daughter was born who illuminated the circle of the quarters; she was named Citralekhā. (SurSūCa.35 [p.
Immediately thereafter, the queen gave birth to a son indicated by beautiful dreams; on an auspicious day and under favorable stars, he was given the name Cittagati.
King Haricandra also [honored] the ascetic named Sumukha.
Having heard the Jina-dharma, which is the cause of the bliss of perfection (siddhi), at Payamūla,
and having established his own son Pahañjana on his own throne, he went forth,
fearing residence in saṃsāra and weary of sensual enjoyments. (SurSūCa 37–38)
Having performed austerities for a pair of months at the feet of the Cāraṇa Sumuha,
he exhausted the web of karma and became an Antagaḍa Kevalin. (SurSūCa 39)
Moreover, the Vidyādhara king Prabhāvilāsa, having abandoned all anxiety, enjoys the kingdom bestowed by his father; he is indeed Jvalanajaṭhara.
And of him, there are two chief queens from among the excellence of his entire harem.
Kalahaṃsī and Mañjūsā were born of a noble lineage;
from Kalahaṃsī was born a son named Jvalanaprabha.
Mañjūṣā’s young son was named Kaṇakaprabha.
Meanwhile, Queen Bandhusundarī, remembering the words of her own brother, realized that her daughter Citralekhā had reached the bloom of youth. (SurSūCa. 42–43)
Then she confirmed those words of her brother to her beloved Bhānugati; and thereupon Bhānugati gave his own daughter,
Citralekhā, to the eldest son of Khaṇḍapatha, who was endowed with beauty.
Then,
with supreme joy, she was married by Jvalanaprabha; and together with him, full of affection, she was led to the city of Suranandana.
Enjoying his domain together with her, he dwells like a god in the celestial realm.
Then, on a certain occasion, Pahañjana, the lord of the sky-dwellers, beheld in the sky a house as white as the moon and radiant as a temple of the gods.
[179] Then Manohara began to think: "Alas! This is the very appearance of this lady; therefore, I shall have a beautiful temple of the Jina built. (SurSūCa.48)
As soon as the king had diligently drawn [the image] upon the jeweled floor, the entire cloud, struck by the wind, instantly dissolved.
Seeing it dissolved in an instant, the king reflected thus: SurSuCa.49. Having seen that it had dissolved in a moment, the king reflected in this way.
In this way, for human beings, fortunes are of a fleeting nature;
just as this cloud-mass was seen in one moment and then vanished again, so too all objects of experience produce joy for only a moment. (SurSūCa 50–51)
Form, life, youth, and even all one's kinsmen and relations are thus impermanent; alas! Fie upon dwelling in saṃsāra!
For even though they know directly that it is impermanent, people still regard it as stable.

The non-existence of objects is their existence; this is the incapacity for discernment. Even having known the words of the Jina, they continue to engage in violence and possessiveness. (SurSūCa. 53) [p. 180]

"Alas! How great is the power of delusion, this attachment to sensual pleasures! Therefore, enough for me of this kingship, which is the cause of dwelling in *saṃsāra* and is indeed rooted in heavy suffering, now that I have come to know the words of the Lord of Jinas. (SurSūCa 54–55)
Therefore, having abandoned what is blameworthy, I shall quickly exert myself in the life of renunciation;
for what use have I for this worthless kingdom, which is a cause for binding one to an evil rebirth? Furthermore, in my lineage, the kingship has been given to one's own sons.
"Many kings who practiced the vows of a renunciant have attained a happy rebirth.
Therefore, this same duty must be performed by me as well, born as I am in that lineage.
Having reflected thus, the king informed the *khecaras* gathered nearby.
In the meantime, the sage Sughosa, a Cāraṇa possessing the four types of knowledge, arrived there while wandering for the purpose of enlightening those capable of liberation. (SurSūCa.
Then King Pahañjana, having bestowed the kingdom upon his son Jalaṇappaha as well as the supreme *pannatti* science upon Kaṇagappaha,
departed from there to the presence of the ascetic Sughosa.
Having abandoned royal splendor, Prahanjana became the king of the sky-dwellers (gandharvas).
Jvalanaprabha also enjoys the glory of kingship, surrounded by a multitude of sky-dwellers;
they all approach him with various offerings preeminent in their excellence. (SurSūCa 61–62)

Kaṇagappaha, having mastered the vidyā named Prajñapti according to the prescribed rite, attained a vast expansion of great power born from the majesty of that vidyā; yet he abandoned the tradition of his own lineage, disregarding the drum of infamy in the world. (SurSūCa 63)
Disregarding the lack of discernment, without considering the descent into a miserable state,
and without reflecting upon the dignity of his elders, he— driven by greed for royal splendor and filled with the pride of his magical powers— thus accepted such ungracious conduct. (SurSūCa 64–65)
[182] Having seized the royal throne bestowed by his father from his elder brother Jvalanaprabha through the power of his magic sciences, Kanakaprabha [ascended it]. (SurSūCa. 66)

Then, having taken over that entire kingdom, the high-spirited Sāmāyika brought the whole multitude of sky-dwellers under his control. (SurSūCa. 67)
Expelled from his own land by his younger brother,
Jvalanaprabha arrived in the city of Camaracañca at the side of his father-in-law.
With great respect, he was ushered into his father-in-law’s city.
Then, at that very moment, by means of a painting, he was brought before King Bhānugati.
O Citravega! While he dwelt there in that city of the gods with supreme delight, several days passed for him. (SurSūCa 69–70)
Then, on another occasion, Jvalanaprabha, accompanied by Sālaka named Citrāṅga, departed from that city. (SurSūCa.

Beholding many kinds of groves adorned with delightful trees, and a multitude of lakes with clear waters frequented by flocks of *bhāraṇḍa* birds; beholding the peaks of the great mountain with their far-spreading white clouds— SurSūCa.72.
In a place made beautiful by a plantain grove where a pair of kinnaras were closely embracing,
delightful with the clamor of sweet-voiced cuckoos crying out in unison, and sweet with the heavy humming of swarms of wandering bees; (SurSūCa 73–74)
In a certain forest bower, filled with trees bending under the weight of their fruit, both Śakra and Citragati arrived at the same time out of curiosity.
(SurSūCa. 75) [A group of four verses].
He beheld a red *aśoka* tree, beautiful with the emergence of fresh sprouts stirred by the blowing wind, and filled with the humming of swarms of bees;
and seated beneath it upon a golden lotus, he saw the eminent sage. (SurSūCa 76)

Being saluted by a multitude of Vidyādharas, Nārakas, Kinnaras, and gods, and being praised by the foremost of the gods, he attained pure, absolute knowledge (vimalakevalajñāna). (SurSūCa. 77, p. 184)
But when Jvalanaprabha drew near, he was recognized by him.
"This is that very father of mine, the eminent sage named Prahanjana"—when this had been told, both of them, Citragati and Harisena, were filled with joy. (SurSūCa. 78–79)
Having thus circumambulated him three times properly, their hair standing on end with intense joy,
they bowed at the feet of the Kevalin and sat down upon the surface of the earth. (SurSūCa.80,
a yugma)
Then, in that assembly, the Blessed One, whose voice was as deep and resonant as the thunder of a cloud that has conquered its own turbulence, began to deliver a discourse.
Furthermore: "The fortune of men is as fickle as the ears of a fighting elephant; human life is impermanent. (SurSūCa.81)

Even the youth of humans is suddenly assailed by old age. Furthermore, in this world of living beings, even that youth becomes afflicted by hundreds of diseases for some, and by the suffering of separation from the beloved and union with the unloved. (SurSūCa.82–83)
In this transient youth of living beings, which is filled with immeasurable diseases, clusters of ailments, sorrows, and calamities, what indeed is the cause for attachment? // SurSuCa.84 //
Sense objects, which are the cause of miserable rebirths, are likewise trivial when enjoyed; they too become bitter at the end.
Therefore, what attachment can there be for them?
Thus, in this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), whatever appears to be essential is merely a false hope.
Knowing that even this is difficult to obtain, practice the Jina-dharma.
This assembly, which is so difficult to find and which you have attained— having never before reached it within the ocean of existence— do not let it go to waste here.
Indeed, this [human birth] is difficult to obtain again for those wandering through existence, which is crowded with millions of births;
there is no other refuge for them except the teaching of the Jina.
Therefore, having taken up the initiation and practiced self-restraint as taught by the Jinas—*SurSūCa.88*—[one should strive].
Having abandoned the cycle of existence, one attains the supreme happiness of perfection.
When the Sage had thus explained the Dharma, some there took up the life of a renunciant.

Then the Kevalin said, "It will happen; when?
He was asked this, and then the lord of sages, who had realized the ultimate truth through his kevala-knowledge, replied:
"O blessed one, when the *bhānugati-dinna-rohiṇī* spell has been accomplished by you!"
"You shall once again become the lord of the sky-dwellers; of this there is no doubt.
(SurSūCa 93) When the sage had spoken thus, the Blessed One was saluted by those with smiling faces.
In the meantime, the entire assembly departed as they had come. (SurSūCa 94)
Then those two people quickly arrived together in their own city,
and Citragati related the words of the Kevalin to his father.
Then, on an auspicious day and under a favorable constellation, the Rohiṇī-vidyā was bestowed simultaneously upon both the daughter and the son-in-law.
And they were instructed: "Perform the preliminary service (*pūrvasēvā*) correctly according to the prescribed ritual procedure."
Having remained in the *vasima* (the inhabited area) for the period of six months, thereafter, the fierce *uttarasādhanā* must be performed by those who are solitary in the forest; furthermore,
one must exist in the form of an assistant (*sādhakarūpa*) to the *uttara*.
"Even in terrifying and frightening circumstances, one must not give up hope;
in the seventh month, when the merit is ripe, the science (vidyā) will grant its vision.
Thus addressed by the king, both [the queen and the minister] bowed at his lotus-feet.
They began to perform it for six months until it was completed. Then, in the seventh month, having gone into the forest, that entire ritual procedure—
including the fire-offerings and so forth— was previously undertaken by Jvalanaprabha.
Vasunanda, the wielder of the sword and protector of his mind, became his guardian;
he too, with undivided intent, began to carry out that slaughter. (SurSūCa.102)

On the day of the alms-round, Citralekhā was seen at that place, rushing forward in haste with her body trembling, terrified with fear. Seeing his own sister, Cittagati said: "Where have you been, my dear?"
"O sister, why have you come alone to this most terrifying forest?
Out of fear of whom do you tremble so violently? She replied to him:
"I have come out from the city surrounded by female servant-maids."

Having arrived there in the garden, I worshipped the Flower-Arrowed One (Kusumabāṇa). As I was returning to my own home, I was suddenly rendered unconscious by someone; leaving that retinue behind, I fled and have come here.
Then, in the forest, I suddenly beheld Kanakaprabha.
That wicked man said, "Desire me," as she was intensely enraged.
Then he reviled me excessively with harsh words;
having drawn his sword, he said to me, "Submit to me! I replied, "No; otherwise, I shall cut off your head with this sword. (SurSūCa.108–109)
And when she had been addressed thus by him, trembling with fear as she fled, she reached your presence, saying, "Protect me from that wicked woman!
As she was speaking thus, he suddenly approached and seized her by the hand.
The sun, dark as a tamāla leaf, arose in the sky.
Seeing his own sister being carried away while she was lamenting thus—"Alas! Save me, save me, brother! Alas, beloved! Grant me protection!"—[he rushed forward]. (SurSūCa. 111–112)
"O bringer of disgrace upon your own family! Where have you fallen into the range of my sight?
Be a man; I shall cut off your head! [SurSūCa.113] (p.
Calling out these words, Citta-gati, grasping his sharp sword, flew up along the path in order to liberate his sister. (SurSūCa. 114) [A group of three verses]
Then, while he was thus bewildering him, Kaṇagapaha arrived in his own city;
Citragati, the sky-walker, also reached him following along that same path.
Then, having bewildered Citragati with the *vimohana* spell, [Kaṇagapaha...]
Surānandaṇa entered his own city, Kaṇakapura.
Then Citragati, his mind deluded and having forgotten the abduction of his sister, descended there into the outer garden out of curiosity.
Having seen the multitude of people gathered at the festival time in the magnificent temple of the Lord of Jinas, Usabha,
resplendent in their various garments,
he entered the temple of the Lord of Jinas and, with devotion, paid homage to the First Lord of Jinas.
Seated in the midst of the host of Vidyādharas, Citragati remained there when,
in the next moment, a certain man dispatched by Jvalanaprabha arrived.
Inquiring about Cittagati in the temple of the Jina,
Damaghosa saw her; having seen Cittagati, he bowed, led her aside, and then spoke for the sake of his sister's liberation.
Then you were born as Jvalanaprabha; even upon seeing all of that, your mind remained undisturbed, and you did not at all waver from your own duty. (SurSūCa.
122 [Yugma])
Seeing his mind unshakable and his path toward the fire, that Rohiṇī-vidyā, through the practice of mantra-recitation, suddenly became manifest before him.
She said: "O son! Your fortitude is indeed truly peerless."
"I am accomplished for you; tell me what must be done by me.
Jalaprabha said: "My wife, who was carried off by Kanakaprabha, has been taken away;
bring her back to my side immediately."
Then the Vidyā said: "Listen now to this matter, my son; indeed, the entire account of that [incident] comes from the words of the Kevalins. (SurSūCa.126)
He was described in the *Pannatti*; therefore, he has come into your presence.
All this was done by him through deceit for the purpose of provoking you.
(SurSuCa.127) [Yugma]
Your wife remains in her own home, free from affliction and living in comfort;
but Cittagati, deluded by that [demon] through the power of the *mohana* spell,
dwells settled in the temple of the Lord of Jinas in the city of Suranandana.
"Therefore, my son, do not feel any distress regarding this matter!
Having spoken thus, the Vidyā immediately vanished from sight. (SurSūCa.129) [Yugma].
"I have been dispatched by Jvalanaprabha to your presence.
When he had spoken thus, Cittagati, his mind undeluded, set out with Damaghosa toward his own abode. (SurSūCa.130–131)
[193] In the meantime, when the ablution of the Supreme Victor had been mostly completed, the people entered the city mounted upon various kinds of vehicles. (SurSūCa. 132)
Furthermore, some were mounted on palanquins,
others on excellent chariots, on elephants, horses, mules, and various types of litters and yokes.
In the meantime, there appeared an elephant, as vast in body as it was radiant with the brilliance of gold.
Intoxicated and deluded, he was driven out from that city.
Breaking down the doors of houses and shouting repeatedly at the crossroads, he killed multitudes of people and disregarded various secret matters. (SurSūCa.134–135)
Then, seeing him— who resembled the god of death, who held up his trunk with great weight, and whose mouth was most terrible— the world, terrified by the fear of death, fled in every direction.
He too, indeed, shattered the multitude of chariots with blows from the tips of his tusks.
Licking his trunk, he wandered everywhere there;
out of curiosity, he stood in the sky and began to look about.
Like a rutting elephant following its own course, or like the word of Death, it is difficult to perceive.

In this very interval, within a single excellent chariot, there was a young woman at the onset of her first youth, of incomparable beauty, adorned with many kinds of exquisite ornaments. (SurSūCa.138–139)
When the chariot was wrecked by the horses that had strayed onto the wrong path and by the elephants standing in its way, she fell to the ground like one whose life has departed.
[Yugmam] (SurSūCa.140)
Her wide, tremulous eyes were like fresh blue lotuses;
her excellent braid of hair was disheveled, and her earrings had slipped from her ears. Her girdle-string, with its cluster of broken golden tinkling bells, hung down in tatters.

With their breasts barely concealed by the *īṣīkā* grass, the flowers from their heads fallen away; with their upper and lower garments disarrayed, their waistbands slipped off, and their necklaces scattered;
their bodies adorned by pearls falling from broken strings of necklaces. (SurSūCa 142–143)
[195] Then that elephant saw her with her pair of anklets shattered, her own jeweled necklaces crushed to pieces, and her body lying upon the surface of the earth. (SurSūCa. 144)

Then, with his trunk raised, the noble elephant moved toward her as she stood there;
seeing him, the attendants around her raised a heavy cry of "Alas! Alas! (SurSūCa. 145).
She was a young woman with well-knit major and minor limbs, a face like the full moon,
a waist so slender it seemed graspable by the hand, and broad hips.
Even though she saw the elephant approaching nearby, she was unable to move away.

[Three verses as a *kulaka*] Alas! Alas! The jewel of a woman, the treasury of desire, perishes;
having descended from the sky, she was seized by them in their embrace. (SurSūCa. 149)
Having herself suddenly taken him, she led him to a place free from danger and set him down upon the lap of a stone slab in the cool shade of a tree. (SurSūCa.150)
Then,
as she was being consoled by her female attendants, he was gazed upon by her with eyes closed in bashfulness and trepidation;
then, seeing that young man as if he were long-familiar, [she was overcome] by a state of great affection and sincerity.
Sprinkled with nectar,
her cheeks blossomed; and having beheld that incomparable form, whose movements were as swift as thought, he remained with his eyes fixed motionlessly upon her face.
Just then, her nurse, accompanied by several young women, arrived quickly and sat down; she addressed him with sweet words:
SurSuCa.154 [Yugma]
"Those who are devoted to performing the tasks of others are indeed called 'true friends' (sajjana)"—this golden maxim was proven true by you while rescuing the lord of elephants.
(SurSūCa. 155) [p. 197]
"O you whose love is without cause! By your power this life of mine has been saved.
Having thus rejoiced with many such reflections, she spoke again:
"I shall go to our home, for it is now past noon."
And it was said by Cittagati, "Do so," and then,
as they were setting out toward their own city, that maiden quickly took the seal-jewel from the palm of Cittagati’s hand.
Then, having secretly entrusted him with that which was fixed upon her as her destiny,
she, her body trembling with fear, set out to go;
she turned her neck back, her gaze betraying her exceedingly heavy passion.
He meditated upon her in such a way that she became the object of his flower-arrowed passion.
Then, accompanied by her circle of friends, she gradually entered her excellent city; and even Citta-gati had his heart captivated by her youth and beauty.
Seeing him born as if from the mind itself, having ceased all other activities in an instant, Damaghoṣa spoke thus with great humility: [SurSūCa.162]
[In a pair:
"The sun is now reaching the peak of the mountain, its heat having faded; therefore, O Prince, let us go to our own place—what is the use of this delay? // SurSuCa.163
Having heard those words and having assumed the restraint of a householder, he said: "We shall do exactly as you say; however, this is the reason for our delay:
a precious gem fell from my hand somewhere here."
"Having searched for him, I will return here immediately at dawn. "Therefore, go quickly and report the news to Jvalanaprabha.
Then, smiling slightly, Damaghoṣa spoke thus: (SurSūCa.166) 166.
"O Prince, even though it was seen with your own eyes, what is the use of these evasive words here? Did you not see the maiden grasping your hand? (SurSūCa.167) [p.
"It is proper to set aside that morsel and speak exactly as it is; I shall return after obtaining the girl's fundamental purity.
When he had spoken thus, Citragati laughed and replied:
“O Damaghoṣa! You have correctly understood that which was in my mind.
Having thus spoken, he made his salutation, flew up, and reached his own place;
then, with the speed of thought, he entered the beautiful temple of the Jina from the beginning of time.
Having gone to a secluded place where there was no obstruction from other Jinas, he sat down before the image of the venerable Lord of Jinas; by that time, the night had already arrived.
Then he began to reflect: "What, I wonder, has she done with my hand? (SurSūCa. 171a)
"Have I grasped a jewel of a maiden, or have I washed away my own [merit]?
What indeed must I know of her lineage, and how is she to be chosen as a bride?
If she should exist—if she should be such a woman—then life would be fruitful. (SurSūCa.172–173)
For one endowed with such beauty, the enjoyment of sense-objects here is appropriate; in their absence, even the craving for sense-objects is but a mockery, which I shall now cast away. (SurSūCa.174)
That man whose palm she would cling to— she who has the gait and movement of a swan, and arms as delicate as the interior of a plantain shoot— is truly blessed;
for by that very thought, "I am fortunate," I have taken that slender-limbed woman upon my lap.
And because she embraced me so tightly, she was not deceived by me.
Furthermore, should there be a journey again, when she has fallen to the ground in fear of an elephant, let her be seized by him and suddenly pressed against him firmly. (SurSūCa.176–177)
While he was thus reflecting with many variations of thought, his mind fixed upon that [goal],
the night passed away along with sleep, and the sun rose.
Then, at the time of dawn, he first paid homage to the Supreme Jina according to the prescribed ritual.
He set out toward the city to visit the houses of his kinsmen;
having reached the city, he saw it devoid of people, with all its white mansions empty.
Having seen that city abandoned by Fortune, like a deserted wilderness, he, with a heart filled with wonder, thought to himself:
"Alas! From where has this city suddenly become desolate? (SurSūCa 180–181)
Could this be Indra’s sport, or is it indeed a real Urvashi?
Has she been carried away from this place by an angry god?
Or has the people fled from this city out of fear of someone? (SurSūCa. 182)

While he was reflecting thus, his mind entered [deep thought] until— just then— a certain man was seen approaching from the direction of the sea; with due courtesy and in a sweet voice, he spoke this to him.
[In three stanzas, forming a *kulaka*:
"O gentle-faced one! For what reason has this excellent city of Uvviśaya been suddenly set on fire? Then he said: "Listen as I explain it. (SurSūCa.185)
[202] This is well-established: the heroic King Kanakaprabha, proud of his mastery of the sciences, protects this excellent city as the king of the sky-dwellers. (SurSūCa.186)
Having usurped the royal throne bestowed by his father from his elder brother Jvalanaprabha,
he himself took control here;
and having expelled his elder brother, he went to the city of his father-in-law.
He too remains in this city, enjoying sovereignty.
It is said that his father-in-law, Bhānugati, gave him the Rohiṇī vidyā;
he has mastered it, and the secret of this vidyā was revealed to him.

Then King Kanakaprabha, having gone there to that very place where the obstacle stood, was not shaken by that jewel; rather, he became afraid of it as he was returning toward his own city with a distracted mind. (SurSūCa.190)
Once, due to the power of negligence, he even overstepped the precinct of the Jina temple;
previously,
this rule had been established for sky-dwellers by Dharaṇendra.
Whoever here commits an act of transgression against the temples of the Jinas, the monks,
or the images, his mastery of the sky will suddenly perish;
thus was it made known to all the sky-dwellers on Mount Vaitāḍhya.
[In a pair of verses:
Thereafter, O noble one, because this king had transgressed the temple of the Jina, Dharaṇa, being enraged, instantly brought about the loss of his magical powers. (SurSūCa.194)
Knowing that Jvalanaprabha had attained the vidyā, Kanakaprabha,
deprived of his magic power and unable to remain in this place,
fled; terrified, he went toward the southern path at Gaṅgāvarta.
"O refuge of Śrīgandhavāhana, together with your retinue! [Thus they cried].

deprived of their lord and terrified by fear, they spoke thus to one another: (SurSūCa.197)

"Who will provide protection for us all here, dwelling without our lord? Therefore, it is fitting that this city be abandoned immediately.
Thus was the decision made by the city elders, who were skilled in counsel.
"All the people have perished, and now the city has become empty. Having encountered this situation, Citragati then said to Urvashi: "O noble lady, where has that person gone? (SurSūCa.200–201)
Then he said: "Some person has gone to the city of Gaganavallabha, some to Vijayapura, and indeed some here to Veyajanta;
some have gone to Sattuñjaya, and likewise some people have gone to Ariñjaya. (SurSūCa. 202)
In the city of Nandana, another was born; in the pure city of Vimala;
in Rathanūpura, one indeed; and in Ānandapura, another who conquered his enemies.
Some indeed went to the city of Śakaṭāmukha, and likewise to Vejayantī;
some to Ratnapura, and some to the city of Śrīnagara; some to the city of Jalāvarta, and some to Saṅkhanābha. (SurSūCa 204–205)
"In the various cities and towns, by means of a summary of his adversaries,
the entire population was scattered like a heap of grain blown away by the wind.
Having spoken thus, that man, having performed his salutation, began to depart.
Then, having suddenly heard those words regarding the course of his mind,
he experienced an unbearable suffering, as if struck by a club on the road, or swallowed by a provoked demon, or as if struck by a thunderbolt.

Even in this vast city, which is crowded with millions of families, right vision is extremely difficult to find for one who does not know the inner recesses of the family home. (SurSūCa.210)
But now, since people have departed for various cities,

Therefore, what shall I do now, since this [hope] has been shattered by wretched fate?
"How might news be obtained, or how might there be a sight of me?
Who indeed should be asked for her name, and who would tell me of her family home? And who would point out that excellent city where my beloved has gone? (SurSūCa. 212–213)
"Alas! That [woman] was seen by us through the power of fate;
now, who knows where she must be seen again? Her syllables have become like a mantra for the demon of separation. (SurSūCa.214)

What hope can you still have, O heart, when you do not even know his whereabouts?
Furthermore, if you must burn, then burn; why do you beat your breast, O heart? I shall certainly not restrain you, for even news of my beloved has now become difficult to obtain.
Or rather, what is the use of this reflection filled with such profound despair?
Having summoned my fortitude, I shall consider some means;
for by applying themselves to a means, men attain their desired goal.
"Sleep comes to those who are sleeping; this is easily obtained in the world.
And here is the method: I shall wander through all the cities of the Vidyādharas; let no one anywhere say even a word regarding my involvement with her. (SurSūCa. 219–220)
Whether as a slave or a mistress, that moon-faced young woman was wandering about in some city, and she was indeed exceedingly beautiful. (SurSūCa.221) [p.

Having thus resolved the matter, O Cittavega, my mountain-like mind—shattered by the heavy sorrow of separation from my beloved and the avoidance of the path of the heart—then, having abandoned my circle of kinsmen, became overwhelmed by intense affection. (SurSūCa. 222)
Alone, I wandered through all the cities in the northern region of the Veyaddha mountains,
yet I did not obtain any news of her anywhere;
from there, I came to the southern Senī.
Having wandered through various cities there and not obtaining what I desired, I have today arrived once again here in your city, Kuñjarāvatta.
And as I was entering this very garden, an auspicious omen occurred.
Then my right arm throbbed and likewise my eye; thereupon I reflected:
"Surely there will be a meeting with that beloved of mine this very day, or perhaps some other most auspicious event."
Reflecting thus, I arrived here at this plantain grove; having prepared a milk-rice porridge, I sat down upon the surface of the paved floor. (SurSūCa.228)
And at that very moment, O lovely one, my sleep departed; having heard your voice, I immediately awoke.
Then, thinking "By whom has this been spoken?", I looked toward all the directions.
And at that very moment, you were seen clinging to the tree-branch.
"Alas! Alas! How can this youth of formless beauty perish while clinging [to it]?"—thinking thus, he raised a cry of lamentation.
He has come into your presence; now the snare has been suddenly cut by me, O Cittavega! Everything else is indeed manifest before your very eyes. (SurSuCa.232) [A pair of verses]
“O noble one! Regarding that which you have asked—how is it that you do not even know the location of your own wife? All of this has now been explained to you. (SurSūCa.233) [p.
Having seen this rare human birth, endowed with beauty and youth, one must certainly not commit suicide for the sake of a female friend.
O Cittavega! Even though the suffering caused by separation from a beloved is indeed difficult to bear...
"Even for those born of the most noble lineage, this is nevertheless not proper. [The King said:
"I too know this: for a human being who is dear to the heart, in separation, a terrible suffering arises, just as it does for a denizen of hell in hell. (SurSūCa.235–236)
"Nevertheless, it is not right to commit suicide; rather, some means must be devised so that she, who is dear to my heart, may be found.
"O Supraṣṭha! thus was it spoken by that Cittagaī.
Sighing deeply, I spoke thus:
"That conversation has passed; indeed, there is no remedy now, for her marriage shall take place this very night. (SurSūCa 238–239)

And I said: "Who is he? He replied: "O noble one, listen!

"After she has married someone from her own family, she will come later. While following that custom, she will arrive for the purpose of worshipping Madana;

Then, when she has arrived, I shall take her own garments and go to the side of the bridegroom in the form of a woman.
Having taken that golden necklace, however, I shall vanish at that very moment.
"I too shall destroy him by means of a stratagem when I have found the opportunity.
For it is only in this way, my dear, that there can be success for her, and not otherwise. [SurSūCa.245, p. 212]
Thus may the word of the deity come true; furthermore,
a man must exert human effort toward his desired goal,
for the accomplishment of the task indeed results from the application of destiny.

When he had thus spoken this appropriate counsel, O Suppaïṭṭha! his mind being utterly deluded by intense passion, he disregarded the heavy suffering that was to come and accepted his words. This fifth excellent chapter, which serves as an illustration of the means for attaining Kanakamālā and is like a water-mantra for quelling the fire of passion and the poison-dragon of hatred, has been told in the *Surasundarī-kathā*. (SurSuCa. 1250)

In the meantime, the sun, having traversed the entire circle of the sky, reached the western ocean, exhausted by his journey and seeking a place for his bath.

Now, for the sake of the purpose undertaken by Madana at his house,
I said, "So be it," and both of us rose and gathered several flowers there in that garden. (SurSūCa.2–3)
Having entered the house of Madana and honored Madana, he spoke thus: "O Blessed One! By your grace, our desire has been fulfilled. (SurSūCa.4 [Yugma])
Having spoken thus, both of them then hid themselves; and when the night had passed for about one watch, and was slightly more than that—SurSūCa.5 [p.
Surrounded by a vast retinue, being sung to with excellent auspicious hymns and accompanied by the sounding of various multitudes of musical instruments,
he was escorted by his own companions and mounted upon a magnificent palanquin.

Adorning their bodies with auspicious ornaments, their limbs decorated with white finery, wearing white garments and smeared with fragrant pastes, they arrived at the gate of the House of Desire, garlanded with golden wreaths. (SurSūCa. 7–8)

] Having disembarked from the palanquins and taken the articles for worship, they then stationed their entire retinue at the entrance. (SurSūCa.9)

Having fulfilled his desire, she then fell at his feet, sighing deeply with large tears streaming from her eyes. (SurSūCa.11) [p.
With a light voice, this reproachful speech was uttered with a choked throat: "O Blessed One, though you have indeed conquered both gods and men, why do you strike women? // SurSūCa.12 [Yugma]
"O Blessed One! If I have indeed conceived such great affection for this world, why then do you unite me with another world, having abandoned it?
Furthermore, they say that in this world there are only five arrows of yours."
"But as for me, he has become like Sahasrabāṇa. [She said:
"O Blessed One! If you strike me, then strike; who can restrain you?
However, strike me in such a way that I go to the abode of Kṛtānta (Death)."
But you struck me so that I am neither dead nor alive;
therefore, what can I say now, having come to you for refuge?
For one who has been burned by fire, only a physician can provide relief to the world.
With my body tormented by you, I have thus come to you for refuge. If you are pleased with me, grant this boon requested by me.
May I not suffer such a mockery even in another birth. (SurSūCa.18) Let this present birth of mine pass fruitlessly in the hope of a beloved person;
therefore, O Blessed One, grant me that very same beloved even in another birth! (SurSūCa.19)

"O Supratiṣṭha! Having spoken thus, Kanakamālā, her breasts drenched by the flowing streams of thick, falling tears, [placed him] upon that [throne] fashioned from various jewels, which was radiating pure rays of light. (SurSūCa.20)
Then, at that beautiful archway of the inner chamber, she was bound by those women with a noose tied around her neck; she spoke again:
"O God of the Flower-Arrows, I am now dying before you! (SurSūCa. 21–22)
[Three verses as a *kulaka*:
"Let no one say that I have done what is improper," thinking thus, Kanakamālā remained pure for this length of time because of her hope. (SurSūCa. 23)
[217] But now, it is truly impossible for me to break my own vow; yet, leaving aside that beloved of my heart, no other man can hold my hand. (SurSūCa.24)
"O goddesses! They spoke a falsehood; it could never have happened otherwise.
That too must have been brought about by my own misfortunes, O sinful ones.
Or perhaps I was deceived at that time by some deceptive form of a piśāca. (SurSūCa. 25)
"Whether by a flood of water, by food, or by some sky-dweller— O Blessed One,
may there be no obstacle to my desired goal at this time;
through your grace, may my death be accomplished without hindrance."
"Shall death come to me, a sinner whose mind is shattered by the heavy mallet of separation from my beloved, or shall it not? Even now, does my heart still harbor hope?
For even death, which serves to alleviate the suffering of separation from a beloved, is attained only through great merit. (SurSūCa.28)
"If he were here now, I would have achieved my purpose.
Having spoken thus, she suddenly cast herself headlong down.
Having approached the fourth [state], I then severed her bonds. Taking her onto my lap, I then spoke softly to her:
"O gentle one, the Moon, the lord of night, who has conquered the lords of gods and asuras, is pleased with you! (SurSūCa. 30–31)
O dear one! That person, having committed an improper and reckless offense against you, has been brought before you in this very birth by the God of Love.
Let him embrace you firmly around the neck; he is longing for you.
Having been addressed thus, the young girl became downcast with shame. At that moment, Cittagati also arrived at that very place; then I said, "O gentle one, he is now my husband."
O beautiful one! When I was about to take my own life through separation from you, I was restrained by this steadfast man, who is endowed with causeless compassion. (SurSūCa.
"O virtuous one, this means for your attainment has been explained to me;
with this very companion as our support, our desire shall be fulfilled. Therefore, O gentle lady, casting aside that fear which is easily overcome by the nature of women... (SurSūCa. 36)
"Quickly assume all these very same garments so that, O gentle one, he may go outside in your likeness;
for this steadfast man is intent on the welfare of others and would otherwise delude our attendants. (SurSūCa 37–38)
Thus addressed by me, she, with a heart full of joy, performed all of that;
then both of them hid themselves once again behind Madana.
And Cittagati, having completely removed her garment, sat down.
Having flung open the door, he immediately ascended the palanquin.
Then, perceiving that the world of living beings there was silent, I said to that beautiful woman in the palace: "O lovely one, what should be done now?"
With her face cast down, her limbs trembling from the force of her agitation, she somehow managed to speak with a faltering and indistinct voice. (SurSūCa.42)
O Beloved, though tormented by separation from my teacher, I have reached you by a stroke of fortune; do yourself what is fitting, for I have come to you for refuge. (SurSūCa.
43, a yugma)
When he had spoken thus, I married that maiden according to the Gandharva rite, making that god Madana my witness. Then, gradually, I dispelled her fear with various words.
Having enjoyed her for a moment and embraced her while asleep, when sleep had departed, I said: "O gentle one, let us go now;
having conducted ourselves in this manner, it is certainly not fitting to remain here."
Sighing deeply, she then spoke to her beloved of her heart:
"Alas, noble husband! Was my death at all appropriate or timely?
[SurSūCa.47, p. 221]

"O Lord! It was because of me that the fierce Nahavāhana, arrogant in the power of his magic spells, has now entered upon this great calamity. O Master! Even though we are perishing, there is no refuge whatsoever to be found."
But she who appeared as your enemy was, in reality, I myself. O Lord!
While I was tormented by the heat of separation from you, my suffering was not such as it has now arisen upon perceiving your misfortune, O Master! (SurSūCa 49–50)
"O Lord! Though obtained somehow by my great misfortune, you will not remain with me now;
or rather, even what has been attained suddenly perishes for those devoid of merit.
O Supratiṣṭha! Having spoken thus, he clung to my neck.
Then that young girl wept, overwhelmed by the weight of her grief for her teacher.

If death were to come to those deprived of union with you, then there would be suffering;
but now, O beautiful one, even in death there is no suffering for us. (SurSūCa.54)
Furthermore: "Even though this meeting with you has occurred by some inconceivable means, may there never be another such auspicious encounter.
(SurSūCa 55) "Let a remedy be applied; even if it proves fruitless, let it be so—what is the harm?"
"The earth remains exactly as it was for couches and seats.

whatever was appropriate has been seen by me through the power of destiny.

"And we shall make whatever is seen later conform to what was seen at the proper time.
Then,
having paid homage to the Lord of Night (the Moon), he departed from her presence.
Then, clinging to her neck, he flew up into the path of the sky.
Having seen such conduct from men blinded by the darkness of passion,
the sun suddenly rose, dispelling the gloom from afar.
Then she said to him: "O Lord, I am intensely thirsty;
my throat is parched even now. How far away is that city from us?
"O beautiful one, the city is still far away; [stay] here in this forest thicket."
"Let us go; there will surely be water here," I said.

"O Supraṣṭha! Thus I shall rest for a moment until that sound from the nearby pleasure-house is heard.
