Having heard this sound, this reflection arose in him:
"Surely this sound belongs to one who possesses a mind; it cannot belong to anything else in this forest thicket.
Or rather, what possibility is there for such a being to exist here? (SurSūCa 67–68)
Thinking thus, Cittagati quickly emerged from those dense plantain groves together with the young women. Having gone from there, he was embraced by me with affection and joy.
I too sat down right there with him; both of us remained in that very place. Then, having been led out from the house of Madana, I said to him:
"Friend, what have you done? How is it that your retinue has been utterly deluded?"
"Tell me, how did you escape? Who is this woman of such enchanting appearance, and where has she come from? Tell me all of this. // SurSuCa.72 //
Then Cittagaī said: "Listen, O Cittavega!
Having become single-minded, I first went out [to see] the form of Kaṇagamālā. Mounted upon a palanquin, I arrived in due course at her presence."
Amidst a tumultuous clamor of various excellent auspicious songs sung by throngs of *vidyādhara* maidens, my hand was joyfully grasped by Nabhavāhana as he approached; thereafter,
the marriage ceremony proceeded in due order.
In front of Nahavāhaṇa, a dance adorned with various graceful gestures was commenced by the courtesans, accompanied by excellent songs.
At that moment, a certain young woman approached and [placed] her own hand... [SurSūCa 76]...into his palm.
Filled with great alarm, she showed me the seal-ring together with the gem.
Upon seeing it, I thought: "This is that very seal-ring belonging to me."
When that girl, terrified by the fear of the elephant, was seized, I drew out a very large jewel from her thumb; then she was looked at, and suddenly she was recognized. (SurSūCa. 78–79)

This is that very same great beloved who was liberated from the fear of the elephant; how is it that, by the decree of Fate, she has now become my wife? Behold, how suddenly even this most difficult-to-attain thing has come to pass through my sight!
"Or perhaps fate is favorable; what indeed will it not bring about?
Having reflected thus, I showed her my own hand, joined with the ring that had previously been given to her.
Having become her close companion, she reported this to her:
"It is said that Kanakamālā’s head is suffering from a headache.
(SurSūCa.83)
"She has fallen asleep for a moment in the Ashoka grove;
you who are staying here may remain as comfortably as you wish. But when the performance begins, we must be informed immediately. (SurSūCa. 84)
When she had spoken thus, O Cittavega,
I was raised up by her to that place which was like a supreme house and a crest-jewel of a garden, delightful with the nectar-joy of the blossoming juice of fragrant flower-clusters. (SurSūCa 85–86)

Having arrived at the delightful Aśoka grove, he sat down with joy upon the seat offered by her; she too stood before him. (SurSūCa.87) Then, filled with trepidation, she was unable to say anything at all.
O Cittavega!
All of my own history that I previously told you has indeed been recounted by me here in brief, up until the point where I arrived in this female form. (SurSūCa.88–89)
"O beautiful one! In separation from you, I have experienced great mental anguish;
for your sake, I have wandered through all the cities of the sky-dwellers. (SurSūCa.90)
Casting aside shame, tell me:
what is your name, in which family was your birth, and what is the name of your father? How have you come here to this city, into the midst of so many people? (SurSūCa 91)
"O gentle one, how have you recognized me even in the form of a woman?
Thus addressed by me, the young girl somehow cast aside her trepidation and, with her words faltering slightly,
began to speak as follows.
"Come here, my beloved! I shall tell you everything that you have asked.
First, there is the city of Suranandana, which is indeed well-known to you.
There lived a famous king of the sky-dwellers named Prahajaṇa."
And his preeminent minister was highly skilled in the treatises on statecraft,
deeply devoted to his lord, and endowed with a fourfold intelligence.
In former times, Mēhanā was the object of the king’s trust; his excellent wife was a devoted woman, endowed with beauty and grace.
She was born of a noble family and was named Indumatī. While the Lord of Men was enjoying sensual pleasures with her,
a handsome son was born to him, named Aśanivega.
Having mastered the arts and sciences, a repository of virtues, and a source of joy for his parents, he gradually attained youth. (SurSūCa.
99) Furthermore, in this southern direction, at Kuñjarāvarta...
In this very city, there was an excellent sky-goer (gandharva) named Candragati.
His wife was named Madanarekhā, dear to his heart;
in time, a son named Amitagati was born to them.
[230] Her daughter, Campakagaurī, was born after her; named Campakamālā, she reached youth, becoming a captivator of the hearts of the Vidyādhara princes. (SurSūCa.102)

Then that Campaka-garland maiden was chosen in the city of Suranandana by Aśanivega, the son of a minister; she was married to him with great ceremony. Together with that large-eyed woman, he was led back to his own city.

Devoted to the suffering of others, he enjoyed human pleasures. Then, on another occasion, the Great Being, having become weary of that state of mind, [left] the position of minister to his own son, Aśanivega.
Accompanied by King Pahañjana, that Meghanāda, having conceived a profound sense of spiritual urgency,
was ordained as a monk at the feet of the Great Teacher.
Asanivega, the sky-goer, [was likewise ordained] along with his beloved wife Campakamālā.
He experiences the fruit of living as a householder, which is the pleasure of the senses. Then, in due course, five sons were born to Campakamālā.
"Listen, my beloved! These are their names in order:
Vajragati, Vāyugati, Candra, Candana, and Susīha.
I was born as the daughter above these five sons. (SurSūCa.108–109)

On the day of my birth, out of great affection, my father joyfully caused a magnificent festival to be celebrated, surpassing even the festivities for the birth of his other sons. When the twelfth day had passed, he gave me the name Piyaṅgumañjarī.
Having been raised in due course, as our bodies grew,
we brought joy to our parents; cherished by the five nurses,
we reached the state of maidenhood, bringing delight to the eyes of our attendants and the people.
[In a pair:
Then, having gradually mastered all the arts such as dancing suitable for young women, I reached my first youth. (SurSūCa. 113)
Accompanied by my very affectionate friends, I delight there in various pastimes involving the painting of excellent and wonderful pictures, dancing, perfumes, and lutes.
And there, O beloved Yama, by my very nature I was born as a woman seeking men; and many excellent suitors come there for me from among the foremost of the sky-goers.
My father himself tells me of their superior beauty, arts, and prosperity. (SurSūCa. 115)
When no great desire arises for anything whatsoever, then one restrains it. Whichever boon comes, I do not desire it; at that time, my father Aśanivega entered into me. (SurSūCa. 116–117)
Seeing him so sorrowful, Campakamālā said to her own husband:
"O Lord, why do you appear so sorrowful and so deeply overwhelmed by anxiety?
Then he replied: "My daughter has now reached the prime of her youth."
O beautiful one, he does not desire any boon whatsoever; rather, this anxiety is heavy:
that his daughter has reached youth, remains without a husband, and dwells within the family home.
He does whatever he can to bring disgrace upon his family.
"Who might be a suitable husband for my daughter? Alas!
My heart's desire!"—thinking thus, Sudarśana, sleep does not come to me even at night while I lie on my bed. (SurSūCa. 120–121)
Having reflected on these words, O handsome one, that Campaka garland— my mother for my sake— became exceedingly filled with grief.
On another day, at the time of dawn, my dear friend named Dhāriṇī...
The daughter of Sujāpa came into my presence and said:
"Tell me, dear friend, why do you appear today as if your heart were being sold, stolen, or lost? You seem distracted, with a pale face and full of sorrow. (SurSūCa.123–124)
"O dear friend! Although I have come after a long time, why have I not been greeted by you?
Therefore, tell me the cause of this grief that has arisen for you. // SurSuCa.125 [p.
And when my dear friend had spoken thus, I then replied:
"O Dhāriṇī, listen well to the account!
O dear friend, having sported with you during the evening hour..."
Having gathered at their own home for various kinds of play,
they then lay down upon an excellent couch made of gold and various jewels and gems on the upper floor,
covered with a fine swan-feather mattress.
Then, at the hour of midnight, having heard the sound of kettledrums,
she awoke and beheld the path of the sky crowded with divine celestial chariots.
Having seen the host of gods there, who illuminated the entire circle of the sky— SurSūCa.129.
"Accompanied by a host of beautiful goddesses, such thoughts as these arose in me:
'Where have I ever seen celestial chariots like these? And where have I ever seen gods and goddesses of such a kind? (SurSūCa.130–131)
Reflecting thus, dear friend, I fell into a swoon; upon emerging from that swoon, the recollection of my former births arose within me. (SurSūCa.132)
O Dhāriṇī, listen as I relate to you in its entirety these two previous births that I have recollected, both connected with humans and gods. In Jambudvīpa, on the northern side of Mount Sumeru...
In this world, there is the excellent field known as Eravaya, renowned throughout the three worlds.

And within its central region, in the land of the Aryas, there was a preeminent city whose beauty was like that of Amarapura (the City of the Gods), and which was difficult for rival kings to approach.
The abode of the Fortune of the Three Worlds, served by thousands of wealthy patrons,
vast and established for all time— by its very name it is called Suppaïṭṭha.
(A yugma) [SurSūCa.136]
He surpassed the wealth of Dhanada, was devoted to assisting the entire world, intent on worshipping the gods and teachers, and full of affection for his kinsmen. (SurSūCa.
In that place lived a merchant named Haridatta, who was the leader of an entire caravan of traders and was distinguished by his generosity and compassion. (SurSūCa.138,
a yugma)
His wife was Vinayavatī, who had conquered the beauty of Rati, was virtuous, sweet-spoken, skillful, dear as life, and modest.
While he was enjoying the fivefold objects of the senses together with her, [he lived].
Then a preeminent son named Vasudatta was born, who became highly renowned.
Subsequently, three daughters were born in due course to Vinayavatī, endowed with a beauty that surpassed even the splendor of the goddesses of the gods. (SurSūCa 140–141)
The eldest was Sulocanā, the second daughter was named Anaṅgavatī, and the third was named Vasuvarṇā, who was like a wonder of the three worlds;
growing up in succession, they were beautiful and capable of intoxicating young men. (SurSūCa.142)
Then all three of them reached the onset of fresh youth;
that maiden Sulocanā was married in the city of Mekhalāvatī.
By the merchant named Subandhu, the son of Sāgaradatta,
[she] was married as the maiden Anaṅgavatī to the caravan leader Dhanabhūti’s son, named Dhanavāhana, in the city of Vijayavatī. (SurSūCa 144–145)
That very daughter of Vasumati, the princess Mehalāvati,
was married by Dhanapati, the son of Samudradatta. Now,
that merchant Dhanapati was skilled in the arts and possessed a form like that of the god of love.
For a time, however, he enjoys human pleasures with Vasumatī;
they enjoy the fresh delights of the senses, their affection increasing, their hearts mutually devoted, and both in the prime of youth. (SurSūCa.147–148)
The days passed for those who were devoted to the service of their elders, free from the suffering of mutual separation, and who brought joy to their circle of kinsmen. (SurSūCa.149 [a yugma])
[238] Then, on another occasion, the merchant Dhanapati was sleeping on an excellent terrace together with his wife Vasumatī. (SurSūCa.150)
On a night illuminated by the rays of the stainless moon, during the last watch when sleep had faded, that noble and innocent Vasumatī awoke.
Seeing a man other than her own husband sleeping upon her bed, she was struck with fear.
Then, like a slender creeper struck by the wind, she suddenly trembled.
That deer-eyed woman thought: "Where has my own husband gone? How has this man entered the house at a time when sorrow has entered?"
Or could that husband have been killed by this wicked man? That very husband appears to be someone else; is there some kind of delusion?
Or rather, he certainly cannot be my husband; this is certain.
This person appears to be some kind of unprecedented being, acting like a divine apparition;
for he enters another's house and sleeps there so very confidently.
"Surely this must be due to some cause or other.
Even if this is another man or a suitor, it is nevertheless appropriate for me now to quickly tell my daughter-in-law exactly what has happened. (SurSūCa 156–157)
"But if I do not tell this news to my own daughter-in-law somehow,
then for me there will be a stain that is difficult to endure even for the rest of my life.
Having reflected thus, that young woman descended from the terrace.
And she arrived in the presence of her mother-in-law, Sudarśanā.
She was gently raised up, and [Sudarśanā] asked, "Daughter-in-law, what is the reason for your coming?
Thereupon, Vasumatī explained everything exactly as it had happened.
Sudaṃsaṇā said: "There is no possibility of another person being here;
this delusion of yours must have arisen from the influence of sleep.
(SurSuCa.161) [p. 240]
And Vasumatī said, "Mother! You yourself must investigate this.
Thus addressed by her, Sudarśanā went there quickly.
She thoroughly examined that man who was sleeping there in deep slumber.
"This is certainly not Sudarśanā; as this man cannot be my son.
Then Sudarśanā cried out with a long-drawn voice:
"Run, run, people! This is some extraordinary man! (SurSūCa.163–164)
"Surely a paramour has entered our house like a thief"—having heard this clamor made by Sudarśanā, [the people cried]:
"Hey! Seize him! Seize him! Run! Where has he gone? Where does he remain hidden?"
Crying out these words, the entire retinue rose up;
a great multitude of people gathered, saying, "What is this? What is this?
Then the merchant Samudradatta said, "O dear one! By whom have you been robbed?"
He too, having risen from his bed and hearing the clamor, exclaimed:
"Mother, who has robbed you, that you speak thus? // SurSuCa.168
"Indeed, no one of wicked mind is seen here; why, O mother, are you so distressed?
When addressed thus by him, Sudarśanā spoke as follows:
"Who are you? Whose son are you? Why have you come to my house, O wretch!"
"Alas! Shame! For what reason do you address me as 'Mother'?
Why, O you who have lost all sense of decorum, are you sleeping here on my son’s bed?
Where has my son named Dhanavāhin been taken by you, you wretch! // SurSūCa.170–171 //

Having thus heard those harsh words, that man was astonished in his heart and gazed repeatedly at his own body. After looking at his own body for a long time, he, with a darkened face— SurSūCa.172— [gazed] until...
Then, with his mind arising, he suddenly gazes at the vault of the sky,
as if bestowing a boon through an excellent spell that utters the indistinct sound "buḍa buḍa."
And he leaps repeatedly upon the surface of the earth like a frog;
in an instant, he becomes wretched like a *khecarakumāra* who has lost his supreme spell, his body trembling violently, appearing as if insane or as if possessed by a spirit. (SurSuCa.174–175)
Upon seeing that man of such appearance, Sudarśanā said: "O most wicked one! Why do you not say where my son has been taken by you?
Even as she spoke, he remained with his face turned downward and did not speak.
Then that crowd of people began to speak in various ways:
"This man has come to the house of a merchant by stealth, greedy for wealth," others said, "If he is a thief, then why is he sleeping on the bed? (SurSūCa 177–178)
She has come here for the sake of Vasumatī, who had committed adultery; others say she is a paramour—if so, why does she call me "Mother"? (SurSūCa.179) [p.
Therefore, we believe that this very Dhanapati has been transformed by some other deity or dānava into another form for the sake of sport with his beloved.
Others say that he has come here again like a piśāca.
"O, O you of wicked soul, you speak thus for the sake of deceiving us! But listen, others say that it is a deity who has come to test the character of the lady of the earth. (SurSūCa. 181–182)
While people were thus conversing with one another in many ways,
listen, dear friend Dhāriṇī, to what happened there:
[he was] one whose body was enchanting, shining with armlets, necklaces, and earrings.
Suddenly, a god of radiant splendor appeared there.
That god said: "Listen to the matter of this one, O noble ones!
Why do you entertain various conjectures when you do not understand the ultimate reality?"
This very one, a doer of evil deeds, was a sky-farer named Sumaṅgala; he had mastered many kinds of sciences and was highly renowned in the city of the Vidyādharas. (SurSūCa.186)
Then, on a certain occasion, while wandering through desired cities,
he arrived here in the city of Pura, intoxicated by youth. At that time,
Vasumatī had just emerged from her bath and was standing upon the roof-terrace.
Standing in the sky, he watched her for a long time until she had departed.
Having seen her form, his mind was indeed agitated;
then, assuming the appearance of Dhana’s master, he descended here into this house.

Having enjoyed this earth while its ultimate truth remained unknown even by him, this great sinner, his mind impassioned by sensual pleasure, thinks thus: "He stands here in the form of Dhanapati, unknown by the entire world. (SurSūCa. 190)
"With this one of excellent form, I shall enjoy the pleasure of love at this very moment.
What business have I with the Vidyādharīs, or what need have I for other young women? (SurSūCa.191)
"How has this woman, who is a treasury of good fortune, been obtained? Having thought thus, Dhanavatī was carried away by him and,
having been led there, released in the city of Vinītā within the land of Bharata.
Having concealed his own form and assumed the form of Dhanapati, he remains here, devoted to his love for Vasumatī through the power of a vidyā.
That very merchant Dhanapati was also found in the city of Vinītā.
Having seen this unprecedented city, his heart filled with wonder, he reflects:
"What is this excellent city? Where is that city Mekhalāvatī? Has it been carried off by someone? Or am I seeing this in a dream? (SurSūCa 195–196)
While he was wandering thus outside the city, reflecting in this manner, he saw a kevalin who had descended into a magnificent garden. (SurSūCa.197 [p.
Born of the lineage of the supreme Jina Śrī Ṛṣabhanātha, world-renowned and named Daṇḍavirata, that royal sage was accompanied by a multitude of munis.
Seeing him, [the king] felt joy and circumambulated him three times.
Having prostrated at the feet of the Kevalin, he sat down in the appropriate place.
Knowing the occasion, he who had performed his salutation spoke:
"O Blessed One, by whom was I carried away? Or what is this region? (SurSūCa 199–200)

When asked, "What city is this?", the Blessed One then related everything that had previously been told to that merchant Dhanapati. Having learned his true nature, he [realized] that he was destitute of wife, father, mother, and kinsmen.
Overcome by grief for his teacher, he was addressed thus by the Kevalin:
"Do not grieve, O blessed one! Such indeed is this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), overwhelmed by the suffering of separation from the beloved and union with the unpleasant. (SurSūCa 202–203)
O Bhadra! For living beings dwelling in this world whose minds are deluded by sense-objects, unions and separations occur infinitely. (SurSūCa.204)
In ultimate reality, suffering arises from one's own defiled karma; indeed, everything else is merely a secondary cause regarding external objects.
Therefore, that suffering was not ultimately caused by that sky-goer for me.
But thus, within one's own mind regarding phenomena, it is produced solely by one's own karma:
"A coward struck by a stone desires to seize that very stone;
a deer, having encountered an arrow, seeks out the place where the arrow originated. (SurSūCa 206–207)
"Therefore, O noble one! Exert yourself in the eradication of karma according to the command of the Jinas;
then, with your karma dissolved, you shall not experience such suffering.
Thus addressed by the Kevalin, the awakened Dhanapati spoke as follows:
"We desire your favor; O Blessed One, grant me the initiation!
Kevalin granted him the initiation that removes the stain of all evil.

Then he became a śramaṇa, endowed with the qualities of asceticism. Having performed severe penance for three million years, and having observed a three-month fast, he abandoned his body. (SurSūCa.210–211)
He was reborn as a god named Candrājuṇa in the celestial mansion called Candrājuṇa, which is crowded with throngs of apsarases in the realm of Īśāna. (SurSūCa.212,
a yugma)
Then, having learned my entire personal history through the knowledge of [past] births, he said:
"O noble sir! I am that very person who arrived here in this city.
I was seen sleeping on a couch, with my neck resting upon the earth."
Having concealed his own form, he remained there in the guise of Dhanapati.
Anger arose within me, and because of that, I thought: "I shall kill this wicked man while he sleeps with my beloved. (SurSūCa 214–215)
Or rather, having informed my parents and the entire world of this wicked conduct, I shall subsequently carry out his punishment.
Having reflected thus, I stole away all the spells of this wicked man, so that he has returned to his natural state. Then, by means of the earth-goddess, sleep was suddenly brought to an end by me.
When she had woken up, she realized, "This is not my husband; this is another man.
Having gone, she reported the entire matter to her mother-in-law.
Then Sudarśanā, having seen him, became distressed. (SurSūCa.218–219)
Having awakened, he too spoke here to his mother Sudarśanā; having heard those cruel words, he looked at his own body.
Seeing his own body in its former form, he was filled with wonder in his heart.
"By whom has the power of my great spell (*mahā-vidyā*) been stolen today?
Having thought thus, he was about to fly up when he was caught by them.
The supreme *niyavijjā* known as *sambhariyā*, which enables one to travel through the air, was mastered by me.
Nevertheless, when I was unable to fly despite having risen [into the air], I realized in my anger:
"Surely someone has performed the destruction of my magic spell (*vijjāccheda*). (SurSūCa 222–223)
"By that very [fact], he has returned to his natural state; I am unable to fly up into the sky.
While reflecting thus, he fell into a state of dejection.
O dear friend Dhāriṇī! Having heard these words of the god, he... [SurSūCa.224]... thus.
The merchant Samudradatta and his wife Sudarśanā both embraced that deity; their hearts shattered by the most grievous sorrow,
they both began to weep piteously with long-drawn-out sobs.
Thus they wept there with piteous lamentations filled with affection, such that all the people who had gathered there also began to weep. (SurSūCa.227) [p.
Hearing the sound of weeping in the house, every inhabitant of the city, including both the young and the old, gathered there;
and they learned the entire account as it was being recounted from one another.
The women of the city reviled Sumaṅgala in many ways: "May lightning strike him!
May this sinful man not wake up; by which sinner was the innocent Dhanavati carried away? (SurSūCa 229–230)
Alas, wretch! Why were there no celestial nymphs endowed with beauty for you, O foolish Vasumatī, that you should thus violate your virtue?
Therefore, O sinful one, O hellish one, O shameless one, now reap the fruit of your ignoble deed!
The fruit corresponding to one's own conduct is bitter in this world and the next.
This name is not suitable for such wicked behavior;
he who has committed this evil is sinful and inauspicious. (SurSuCa.232–233)
[252] Thus, with harsh and unseemly words, he was reviled in many ways by that people; there the noble one remained, speaking with very dejected words. (SurSūCa.234)
By that very god, those who had been made to weep through illusions were there consoled and properly brought to silence.
Then the god spoke to them as they were shedding a stream of thick tears.
"O auspicious Vasumati! What is there now to encourage your heart?
She replied with her face bowed down in modesty:
"O Lord! Whatever you command, therein lies my encouragement."
The god said: "O beautiful one! If it is so, then take up the renunciation and the Dharma taught by the Jina, which is the uprooter of the great root-stump of karma.
Even though, O beautiful one, this was practiced by you while you were unaware!"
Nevertheless, let this renunciation indeed be his medicine.
Then Vasumatī highly esteemed those words, saying, "So be it."
Then, with great magnificence and with the consent of his own kinsmen,
[he entered] right there in that city, into the mother of the preeminent teacher named Sūdharmasvāmin,
whose feet were served by a multitude of various female ascetics.
Candajasā herself was entrusted by the best of gods;
and by her as well, initiation was bestowed upon Vasumatī according to the scriptural injunctions.
[SurSūCa.242, a triplet]
Even that Sumaṅgala, the lord of the sky-dwellers, was seen by the god with a dejected face; out of compassion, he was not killed at all.
Having been led beyond Mount Mānuṣottara, that excellent one was abandoned there.
Then he, the god, returned swiftly to his own celestial mansion.
And that noble lady Vasumatī, perfectly engaged in the restraints and protections, devoted to self-study and meditation, remained diligent in the practice of humility.
Having practiced excellent asceticism for many hundreds of thousands of previous years, he properly consumed his own body through the process of emaciation. (SurSūCa.246)
Meditating upon that very same excellent deity within her own heart,
Vasumatī, having observed a fast unto death out of devotion, passed away and was reborn in the celestial mansion named Candrāruṇa in the second heaven called Īśāna.
The principal queen of the god named Candrāyuṣa was named Candraprabhā. [This work] is delightful through its collection of beautiful *subodha-gāthās* composed by the virtuous Dhaneśvara,
and serves as a water-mantra for quelling the fire of passion and the venomous serpent of hatred.
Thus concludes the sixth chapter of the *Surasundarī-nāma-kathā*, titled "The Deliverance of the World of Men and Gods.
(SurSuCa.250)
[Chapter Seven] Then, by virtue of a former connection, he met with the god Candrāṅgada.

Intensely attached through deep passion, she enjoyed the pleasures of the heavenly world. (SurSūCa.1) A great deal of time passed for Candraprabhādevī as she experienced divine bliss together with that excellent god in the celestial realm. (SurSūCa.2)
Then, on another occasion, having seen her own husband devoid of luster,
that queen, terrified with fear, addressed the king thus:
"My lord, why do you appear so full of apprehension, as if overcome by dejection?"
"O beloved! Why now do you appear so wretched, as if your body were bereft of luster?
Why have you suddenly bound a mass of flowers upon your head? [SurSūCa.4, p. 256]
"O Lord! Why are your garments now dark-colored?
O Deva, why does your gaze tremble, why is your conduct toward love now so slack, and why do you bend your body again and again? Please tell me! (SurSūCa.5–6)
Thus questioned by his beloved, King Candrāryuṇadeva replied:
"O beautiful one, do you not know why you ask me this?
O gentle lady, at the time of the god’s descent, these signs arise!"
"His death is now imminent.
Having heard these words of her very beloved husband, the queen was overcome with profound grief and fell into a suffering comparable to that of a human being.
Then, on another occasion, while she was looking on, that god vanished from sight like an island tossed up by a fierce wind. (SurSūCa.10) [p.
Seeing her husband deceased, Queen Candraprabhā, overcome with extreme suffering, fainted for a moment and then began to lament piteously in this way:
"Alas! O Lord! O beloved of my life! O King, having abandoned me, where have you gone?"
"O Lord! Abandoned by you, whom shall I take as my refuge? O Master!
Having left me now, where have you gone, O delight of the eyes, that I cannot remain even for a mere moment or an instant without you?"
"That alone is my refuge; that is my lord and my very life, O Deva!
You have abandoned me, O Master! Tell me now, where shall I go?
Alas! Where have you gone, my beloved, leaving me here without a protector?"
"O Lord! Now that you have abandoned me, who is my great refuge?
That very same celestial realm, once graced by thousands of gods and so delightful, now seems like a mere human world to me, bereft of you. (SurSūCa.15–16)
O Lord! This very celestial palace, beautiful, strewn with jewels, gold, and gems, released by you, appears like a jar fashioned by a skilled potter. (SurSūCa.17)
O Lord! Even this group of servants, who are fawning and solely intent on performing acts of etiquette, speaks thus in separation from you, resembling the Paramāhammiya demons:
"The beautiful [city], resplendent with Puṃnāga, Nāga, Campaka, Namēru, and Mandāra trees... (SurSūCa.18)
In your absence, even the garden appears like a forest of sword-leaves (asipattavana).
The beautiful bathing-pools, filled with water devoid of lotuses,
seem to lament in your absence as if they were the Vaitaraṇī river.
"Blessed are those women who follow their husband even into this state of divinity; how could such a thing be possible for me?
Lamenting thus, that queen struck herself with her own hands.
With her limbs suffering great pain, she cries out with a piteous sound;
fainting again and again, she falls to the ground, gasping for breath.
Having regained consciousness, she spoke once more in this way:
"Alas, my Lord! Why do you not look upon me as I lament? Why do you not give me a word? Or are you angry, my Beloved? What wrong have I done to you?"
"O Lord! Though you used to perform thousands of endearments for me when I was affectionately angry, why do you now abandon me as I lament so unexpectedly?
Alas, my husband! Do you not know that I am deluded by exceedingly great passion?"
"How will this great separation come about, by which you have been abandoned so unexpectedly?
Thus, weeping in many ways at the separation from her beloved, she became like an uprooted lotus-pond, her lotus-face devoid of luster.
Seeing that queen overwhelmed by great grief and heavy suffering, her close female companion Sayampabhā spoke to her as follows: SurSuCa.28 [p.
O dear friend! Even though you have known the words of the Jina and have heard the true nature of saṃsāra, why do you lament in this way so excessively, like any other woman?
O dear friend! There is indeed no support to be gained by lamenting excessively.
So, what is the use of this futile weeping that causes your breasts to heave?
Even if you lament a hundred times, beat your body, and give way to great sorrow,
your beloved will still not come— he who was carried away by the God of Death.
Knowing this, loosen your attachment and abandon heavy grief; exert yourself in the religion of the Jina-indra, which brings an end to such suffering.
That form consisting of austerity and self-restraint does not exist in the state of being a god within the cycle of existence.
O beautiful one! For the sake of purifying your right faith, exert yourself!

Having gone to Videha, pay homage to the Lord of Jinas, the Kevalins—the kinsmen of the three worlds—as well as to the steadfast monks who are diligent in the practice of self-restraint. (SurSūCa. 33–34)
Having gone with supreme devotion to the images of the Lord Jinas situated in eternal Jina temples— located on the Kulasekhara island and mountain— pay homage to them. (SurSūCa.35)
Thus, having attained human birth endowed with pure right conviction and having received the initiation of the Jina-variety, they destroy their karma and reach perfection in old age.
Those who have gone there [to the state of perfection] certainly do not undergo such sufferings again.
"You shall remain free from old age, death, disease, and sorrow for all time.
Thus addressed by the self-luminous Candraprabhā, that goddess there abandoned her grief for her husband and returned to this world. (SurSūCa. 37–38)
Accompanied by the self-luminous [goddess], having paid homage to the images of the supreme lords of Jinas,
they then arrived here in Bharata at Nandīśvara; and there,
in the city of Rājagṛha, he beheld them in a magnificent outer garden.
Then, he beheld the Kevalin named Suhaṅkara, who was proclaiming the Dharma— which is practiced by the hosts of ascetics and surrounded by gods, asuras, and humans. (SurSūCa.40)
Descending from the sky together with her dear friend, that goddess—
having paid homage to him who brings auspiciousness and bestows happiness upon sentient beings destined for liberation— SurSuCa.41 [Yugma].
Having sat down in the appropriate place together with that community of monks,
the Blessed One then began to speak thus to that assembly consisting of gods, humans, and asuras, which was profound and majestic: *Suratavijaya-sūtra-caityavandana-bhāṣya*, verses 42–43.
Human birth, birth in a noble family, and the Dharma of the Lord of Jinas—having obtained these, strive in every way; do not be negligent.
This life wanes moment by moment, like water held in the palm of the hand.

Therefore, do not commit negligence regarding the Dharma of the Supreme Jina. Life is like a drop of water clinging to the tip of a blade of kusa grass; strive with the essence of true devotion, for the course of karma is exceedingly treacherous.
Since all suffering in this saṃsāra, throughout the four states of existence, has negligence as its root, therefore this [negligence] must necessarily be abandoned. (SurSūCa 47)
This birth is the cause of disease, old age, and death, and the source of suffering;
under its sway, sentient beings wander in the terrible ocean of existence. Therefore, abandoning negligence, practice supreme exertion for the sake of the Lord of Jinas.
With minds fixed upon this Dharma, which is a ship for crossing the ocean of *saṃsāra* and is the ultimate kinsman, exert yourselves in this Dharma;
having shaken off all evil, you shall then attain the bliss of liberation. (SurSūCa 49–50)

Then that goddess Candraprabhā spoke these words: "O Blessed One! Where has my husband Candrāryuṇa been reborn? What is the duration of my life remaining here, and where will my birth be after I pass away from this place? (SurSūCa. 51)
"Would there be a meeting with him, my own husband?
Thus was he questioned by that queen, who was filled with great respect.
The Blessed One, the Maker of Happiness, then began to speak thus:
"O blessed lady, that husband of yours is right here in this very land of Bhārata,
on the excellent Veyaddha mountain, in the delightful northern region."
In the city of Camaracañcā, he was born as a son from the womb of his beloved wife by a sky-farer named Bhānugati. [Yugma] (SurSūCa.55)
"O Madri, your lifespan was originally eight *palyopamas*;
now, however, only one hundred thousand years remain of your life.
When that hundred thousand years are complete, you too shall cast off [this body] and proceed to that same destination. (SurSūCa. 56)
O blessed one, you will become the daughter of the sky-dweller Aśanivega in the city of Suranandana; there, you will be named Piyaṅgumañjarī, the most excellent,
and you shall have a meeting with your former husband.
[In a pair of verses] [p. 265]:
Then the goddess said: "O Blessed One, how am I to recognize him?"
"When will my marriage take place? she asked.
At that moment, the Kevalin said: "Listen, O blessed lady! When you are released from the excellent elephant by way of a procession for the Lord of Jinas, then [your marriage shall occur]."
"He indeed must be known as that same former lover of mine;
thus, by him, you shall have a special vision once again.
[Yugma] (SurSūCa.61)
Having performed the marriage ceremony of Kanakamālā, your maternal cousin’s daughter,
he will come for the sake of his friend’s business; he who assumes the form of Kanakamālā there is your former lover.
"O blessed Candraprabhā, you must lead him away without hesitation!
Immediately thereafter, there shall be your marriage with him; through the recollection of your past lives, you will remember these words of mine."
[266] Thus, dear friend Dhāriṇī! Having heard the words of the Kevalin, that queen became joyful at heart; she bowed to the lotus-feet of the Kevalin. (SurSūCa.65)
Then, having ascended, she paid homage to all the eternal Jina temples and to all the Tīrthaṅkaras in Mahāvideha; then,
contemplating that very same deity in her mind, she returned to her own place.
Then, on another occasion, she too passed away when her lifespan was exhausted.
While things stood thus, that noble lady Vasumatī and Queen Candraprabhā were in the celestial realm.

O fair-limbed one! I have been born here as the maiden named Piyaṅgumañjarī. Having seen the host of gods today, when the recollection of my former births arose, I remembered that god who was my beloved life-partner in heaven.
O dear friend, long acquainted with me! I am now deeply distressed; my mind is currently overwhelmed by the longing for union with him. (SurSūCa.70) [p.
When will that day come when, with eyes moist with affection, I shall behold that beloved one from my former life, bound by our past love?
How shall he be seen by me soon, and how shall union with him come to pass?
"O dear friend! While I was thus lost in thought, I became overwhelmed with grief. As I remained there, my mind entirely preoccupied with that very thing, you arrived;
yet, though you were present, I did not perceive you, O blessed one, nor did I speak to you. (SurSūCa 72–73)

"O dear friend Dhāriṇī! That which you asked—what is the cause of your grief?—that has been explained to you in its entirety. Then Dhāriṇī said: "O blessed one, the word of a Kevalin is never otherwise!"
"Why do you grieve thus, thinking that it must happen in this way?
Having laughed, I said: "It shall be so; there is no doubt.
Only my mind, O dear one, is made to hurry by great longing!"
In the meantime, O beloved! Campakamālā arrived;
her mother said: "Daughter, eat quickly, drink, and put on your finest ornaments. (SurSūCa. 77)
And I said, "Mother, what is the reason that mealtime has already passed so quickly?
Then my mother said this:
"In the garden, at the temple of the Jina, there will be the ceremonial bathing of the god Yugādīśvara."
When the sun had set with great splendor, the people living there went to witness the ritual bathing;
we too shall go to that very place together with our attendants. (SurSūCa. 79–80)
"For that very reason, breakfast is ready at this morning hour;
therefore, arise quickly and be prepared so that we may go to the temple of the Jina.
Having heard these words of her own mother, she rose up instantly.
Having mounted a magnificent chariot for the purpose of bodily enjoyment and other activities,
and surrounded by his own retinue, he went to that ornament of a garden.

Having properly worshipped in the temple of the Jina, I paid homage to the Blessed One. I beheld the Lord of Jinas being bathed with devotion by the sky-dwellers (gandharvas), while I myself, accompanied by my own retinue, performed the bathing ceremony with abundant wealth. (SurSūCa. 83–84)
Mounted upon his excellent chariot, he proceeded toward the city;
meanwhile, the noble elephant was led out from the city with its eyes wide open.
Seeing that [elephant] rushing headlong toward him, the horses of the great chariot became agitated.
Then, as we set out upon the wrong path, that chariot was wrecked.
I fell to the ground, rendered unconscious by a swoon;
beyond that, O beloved, I know not what happened. (SurSūCa 86–87)
Only this much: you were seen as you departed; having seen you with your own upper garment, a profound joy has arisen in my heart. (SurSūCa.88) [p.
Then, O Beloved, this thought arose in my mind:
"This has indeed come to pass exactly as it was foretold by the Kevalin at that time. Since that [union] was due to our attachment in a previous birth, he is surely my beloved.
The eye delights in this, and the mind bears joy.
(SurSūCa.90) When this is seen, even my body seems as if sprinkled with nectar;
with eyes blossoming, he too appears full of affection. (SurSūCa.91)
While I was thinking, "Surely he will certainly come as my protector," my nurse arrived there accompanied by her attendants.
Having greeted her, she asked me, "O beloved, is it you?"
"Let us return to our own city before the sun sets.
Having spoken thus, they departed from there; and I thought this:
"I have seen my father through my merits; now I must not abandon him."
Except for gazing upon the lotus-face of this one, my vision is submerged in mud; like a weak person, it is unable to move forward. (SurSūCa.95)
Indeed, at such a moment as this, the pair of eyes of any person closes;
like one fallen from an elephant, it becomes a state of suffering difficult to escape. (SurSūCa.
96) Even this nurse of mine has departed, leaving behind this beloved of my heart.
Out of modesty, she said, "I am not able to say anything at all.
Therefore, it is proper for me to take some ornament of his, having observed it, so that my mind may find peace. (SurSūCa.97–98)
"Separated from this beloved of my heart, I have arrived here;
having beheld him once again, I shall steady my own heart.
Furthermore, it is said that he was in the form of a woman at the time of Kanakamālā’s marriage.
"Come, there indeed shall be a meeting with him once again.
Thus was I instructed by that Kevalin regarding this matter at that time.
"And that very same ornament, with its identifying mark, shall be there.
Having reflected thus, O beloved, the seal-ring was taken from your hand at that time and my own seal was given to you. (SurSūCa.101–102)
Having put on that garment, which was permeated with a touch dear to her, she,
along with her retinue, turned her neck and set out toward the city out of great devotion for him.
Then, having become my daughter named Dhāriṇī, she spoke to me.

"This is the singular, established word of the Kevalin. "Then this Devajīva was formerly your beloved. When she had spoken thus, I replied with indignation: SurSūCa.104–105: "This is the singular, established word of the Kevalin. 'Then this Devajīva was formerly your beloved.
When she had spoken thus, I replied with indignation."
"Haṃ haṃ! You have been seen, O Dhāriṇī! Depart from the path of my vision, you who speak such words before me as if they were strung with jewels. [SurSūCa.106, p.
"Why are you not dear now, when previously you were so dear to me?
Then Dhāriṇī, smiling slightly and joining her palms in reverence, said:
"O dear friend! Forgive this offense; all that was spoken by me was untrue."
"Just as before, so now he is indeed dear to you.
But what more can I say? It is the truth: if he is your husband, why have you set out to abandon him?
Therefore, my dear friend, do not be angry; these words of mine are indeed coming true."
Accompanied by her, who spoke many such varied words with smiles, he gradually reached his home; by then, even the sun had set.
Then, for that Dhāriṇī, there arose the recollection of her former births and all past events.
I told this to my mother, and upon hearing it, she was filled with joy.
She, in turn, related everything to my father, named Aśanivega;

then, being delighted, he spoke thus: SurSūCa.111–112: "She told that to my mother, and having heard it, she was thrilled. She also related everything to my father, named Aśanivega, and then, being delighted, he spoke as follows."
[274] A great anxiety arose within me: "My daughter has been born as one who desires men, yet she does not wish for any husband; how shall I manage this? (SurSūCa.113)

"How wonderful is this birth! That she has attained the recollection of her former births is indeed a marvel for us—a true marvel! Water fell upon a sprout that had just burst forth. Furthermore, other men informed me that she was rescued from the fear of the elephant.
"That excellent prince named Cittagati is the son of Bhānumatī.
"I shall give this very one to him, if she has a desire for him?
Then Campakamālā, her heart filled with joy, said this: [SurSūCa.116]

"That prince is indeed my son-in-law; an exceedingly great affection for him has arisen even in this, my excellent daughter. (SurSūCa.117) "But listen, O Lord! [to the story] of this King Kanakaprabha..."
Furthermore, King Bhāṇu and King Gaīṇa have a great mutual enmity;
this is well known to you both, arising from the matter concerning Jalaṇappaha. (SurSūCa.118)
"So, how can I go here to this city for the sake of taking her hand in marriage?
If my daughter is sent to that very city for her svayaṃvara,
O beloved, there will be no joy in my heart."
"If this only daughter of mine is so beloved, then as long as I do not see her married, what is the use of my life? Thus did my mother Campakamālā lament there.
Just then, my brother named Candana arrived and said:
"O Father, why do you remain here so confident and free from anxiety?
For this entire city has indeed become agitated. (SurSūCa.122–123)
Then his father asked, "For what purpose do you know this, my son?
And Candana replied, "Such talk has been circulating in the city."
It is said that when Kaṇagappaharanna was enraged at the Jina temple at Landhika,
a theft of spells (vidyā) was committed by one named Dharaṇinda.
It is further said that the spell named Rohiṇī was mastered by Jalaṇappaha today.
Out of fear of him, King Kanakaprabha fled;
he then sought refuge with Śrīgandhavāhana, the preeminent among those who travel through the sky.
In his absence, this entire city became utterly distressed.
Terrified by the fear of Jvalanaprabha, all the citizens flee; abandoning this city, they depart for various other towns.
And this being the case, O Father, we too must now especially seek to escape.
Thus, having heard the words of his son, King Kaṇagappabha’s excellent minister, Jayanta, immediately ordered his own men:
"Make the necessary preparations for the journey! (SurSūCa.129–130).
[277] By means of his supernatural knowledge (*vijjā*), my father fashioned a magnificent celestial chariot (*vimāṇa*);
and all the family wealth was placed therein by his men. (SurSūCa.131)
And so, my beloved! Dhāriṇī told me all of this, and I too ascended that celestial chariot together with my attendants.
Then that chariot, dark as a sword-blade, soared into the sky.
Having arrived with great speed at the city of Gaṅgāvatta,
he entered there the residence of King Kaṇagappaha;
then Gandhavāhaṇa also performed the appropriate hospitality for him.
"Thus, O beloved, I shall remain at Gaṅgāvatta for some days, contemplating in my heart the means to behold you. And I wonder: when shall I see him again? When will my reunion with him take place?"
"When will the day of Kanakamālā’s marriage take place?"—
thinking such various thoughts there day and night, she remained.
O Lord! Even at night, I find no sleep in separation from you.
On another day, my brother Amitagati arrived there in the city on account of royal business; he was the son of Campakamālā, my mother. (SurSūCa. 137–138)
Having seen Aśanivega, King Śrīgandharvāhana, filled with joy, spoke with great respect:
"Today, for the sake of Nabhovāhana, Kanakamālā has been sought out."
"O noble one! At his request, I too have given this [daughter] to him.
Having determined the auspicious time for the marriage on the fifth lunar day, for her..."
"You must go there accompanied by your own kinsmen.
Then Aśanivega said: "It is fitting for us to go there ourselves;
especially now, according to your word, we must go."
But listen to our reason: our departure is not as it ought to be, because King Kanakaprabha is in a precarious state. (SurSūCa.143)
The loss of knowledge and virtue, the fall from sovereignty, and the abandonment of one's own city—
if he is thus filled with sorrow, how could my going there be appropriate?
Those who do not grieve when another is grieving, and who do not become companions when another has met with calamity— [they are no better than beasts].
Those masters are not truly servants; they should be understood as rogues in the ultimate sense.
Regarding this matter, you should not now insist upon it, even though your sister will come on the wedding day, however anxious she may be.
Then Amiyagati said, "Send Piyaṅgumañjarī;
for because of her, Kanakamālā remains here in a state of longing.
Thereupon, I was dispatched by my father along with my maternal uncle to this place.
And having arrived here in due course, they were reunited with Kanakamālā.
Thus, O beloved, I have come here to the house of my maternal uncle.
"I wonder when the day of my union will come through my merits? For that person whom I must see is dearer to me than life itself.
While she was thinking thus, this fifth [night] arrived.
And when the marriage ceremony had gradually proceeded,
and the spectacle had commenced before Nabhavāhana, I thought to myself: "Indeed,
this Kanakamālā is seen seated here in the midst of her female attendants."
"He, my great beloved, is not seen anywhere here; what then?
Could the word of the Kevalin be false? No, indeed, by my misfortune!
Nay, nay! For even in another direction, the sun somehow does rise. (SurSūCa. 152–153)
Even Mount Meru might dissolve, and all the oceans might reach their end;
yet the states of being described here by the Kevalin can never be otherwise.
"Is this indeed Kaṇagamālā, or is it that beloved of my heart?
By showing this jewel of a ring, I shall make her free from doubt.
Having reflected thus, she came into your presence.
Then my own hand, adorned with the jewel of a seal, was shown to her.
O Beloved! When you showed me your hand bearing the seal, the conviction immediately arose in me: "This is that very husband of mine. (SurSūCa. 156–157)
"Look! Even after doing this, he remains entirely free from fear; why does he not even fear Prince Nahavāhana?
Therefore, I shall employ some stratagem for the sake of his liberation."
Having reflected thus, O Lord, I deceived that entire circle of friends with a ruse and brought you here to this Aśoka grove;
all that you asked has been related by me in its entirety.
[Stanza pair] Even though she is a maiden, O beloved, she cannot in any way be restrained while she is filled with such agitation.
Although not even a single word was spoken in front of Maṇavallabha,
nevertheless I have related this account of my own life in detail; for,
by virtue of your recollection of past births (*jātismaraṇa*), you speak as if you were already acquainted with me.
[In a pair:
"O Cittavega! Having thus heard her words, I suddenly recovered from my fainting spell, and the recollection of my past births arose within me. (SurSūCa.163)
Having related my entire past life as previously recounted, she then said to me:
"O beloved! What should be done now? Thereupon, I replied:
"O gentle lady, your family home is known to me."
"Go home; I too shall flee from here.
"Indeed, Kanakamālā has fallen into this pool of mine by chance; report it thus to all the people with a loud cry. (SurSūCa 165–166)
Thus, when there is no fear for anyone in the agitation of the mind, one becomes liberated from the flow of rebirth; in this way, the excellent friend is truly set free. (SurSūCa.167)
"O beautiful one! Having heard this, and having come to the excellent city of Suranandana, Jvalanaprabha has once again taken possession of his own kingdom.
That excellent city has been restored, and the citizens have been honored by the king. (SurSūCa.168)
Therefore, I shall command your father to go there. King Jvalanaprabha will see you there out of his former affection, and with the permission of your mother and father, I shall marry you.
"And so it shall be, my dear! Indeed, everything will be praiseworthy;
otherwise, however, if this were done, both families would be disgraced.
Then she said to him: "Whatever you command here, I [shall do]."
All that must be done, O Beloved! Listen to my request:
today, O Lord, I have somehow arrived at a state where my life is in peril.
"Except for you, I am not able to go anywhere else now.
My life lasts only so long as you remain within the range of my vision; deprived of the sight of you, however, I shall instantly give up my life. (SurSūCa. 173–174)
I consider even this much—the mere twinkling of the eyes—to be unbearable;
O Lord, how much more so when I must remain for many days in separation from you?
Therefore, O Lord, wherever you go, I too must follow right there.
"Since the matter stands thus, tell me what must be done. Furthermore,
O Lord, if I may go to my own home with such hope as this— that the taking of my hand [in marriage] will take place when I have reached my own place."
Furthermore, even though my father was entreated by King Jvalanaprabha, he did not go at all from his own city, leaving Kanakaprabha behind. (SurSūCa.178) [p.
What could my fate be then? Even the sight of you would not be mine;
let alone the taking of my hand in marriage, it would be far from the joy of my heart. [SurSūCa.179, in three stanzas]

"Therefore, what is the use of much talk, my beloved? I will not let you go from my hands; rather, command me as to what must be done. Thus she spoke, O Cittavega, and I replied: "SurSūCa.180" [End of verse]. SurSūCa.180 bhō cittavēga! ēvaṁ tīē bhaṇiē maēvi saṁlattaṁ.

"If it is so, then O beautiful one, let us depart quickly! [He said: "Before the night fades away, and while the people here, headed by Nabhavāhana, have their minds captivated by the spectacle, let us go, O gentle lady! (SurSūCa.181–182)
And she said: "O Lord, I am standing here before you;
then I suddenly flew into the sky with her. (SurSūCa.
183) And while I was traveling with my beloved for only a short distance...
Then she said: "Pain has arisen in my womb;
my entire body is paralyzed, and an unbearable pain comes upon my heart. (SurSūCa.184)
"O Master! Grant me protection; I am unable to go into this [place].
Then I said to her: "O beautiful one of delicate limbs, you have not even slept during the night, for the wind is exceedingly cold."
"Because of that, pain has arisen in your belly; therefore, do not give way to despair.
I shall quickly descend here into this forest thicket to restore you.
Speaking thus, I descended here into this forest thicket.
Having given my beloved a dwelling here, she was led into a plantain grove.
After rubbing together pieces of araṇi wood, a fire was kindled by me; then my body was consumed in many ways, and after that, I spoke thus. (SurSūCa 188–189)
"O beautiful one! Our bodies are exhausted; let us now go to our own place.
Then she said to him, "My beloved! I shall do so. (SurSūCa.190 [p.
"Thus, O Citravega, both people were led out from the plantain house;
then you were suddenly seen here.
This indeed is Kaṇagamālā’s sister, named Piyaṅgumañjarī."
"O friend! Thus have the arts of service toward you been attained. "O Supratiṣṭha!
All this that was asked by you has been explained by me. Having spoken thus, Citragatin departed. (SurSūCa.192–193)
Then I said:
"O friend! There is no one with a heart as cruel as mine, since out of devotion to my own interest I led you into danger;
yet because of your great nobility, you are intent on accomplishing the task of another. (SurSūCa. 194)
The accomplishment of the desired goal has arisen through the power of your own merit.
Therefore, O friend! There is no one else in the world like you, so selflessly affectionate, by whom even that which is extremely difficult to obtain—union with his beloved—has been brought about.
"Since you have granted me such a life as this by acting in this way, O friend! there is no other benefactor to be found except for you."— SurSūCa.197
Then Cittagāmin said: "What benefit have I done for you?
That alone is a well-done deed which, upon its ripening, is beautiful here in this world. The virtuous do not praise that which is sweet at first taste but harsh in its ripening. (SurSūCa. 198)
"O handsome one, even this appears to me as having an unpleasant consequence, like giving food mixed with poison to one who is hungry;
for Nahuṣa is fierce and arrogant due to the power of his magic spells. (SurSūCa 199–200)
"Alas! In this world, there is enmity over women and wealth that is exceedingly heavy; therefore, my good man, consider how you might indeed achieve deliverance from the king!
Then I said, having reflected upon it: "What need is there for much deliberation here?"
Whatever little may come to pass through my merits—just as this [woman], though exceedingly difficult to obtain, has been attained by me through the power of destiny. (SurSūCa.202) [p. 289]
"Even that which is beautiful shall come to pass as seen by the power of destiny.
Then Citragati spoke thus with a mind of certainty:
"Nevertheless, this stretching out of the feet is indeed not proper."
Then I said: "Since the matter is thus settled, tell me now exactly what must be done in this situation.
Cittagati then replied: "Flight alone is appropriate at present."
"Going to the city of Niyaṇa is not appropriate at this time.
A great delay is occurring while we remain in this place; therefore, O noble one, do not waste any more time now! (SurSūCa.206–207)
Therefore, O friend, you must act in such a way that there is no loss to your body;
from here, I too shall go to the city of Suranandana.
"Having formed an alliance with Jvalanaprabha, I shall enjoy this woman, the beloved of my previous birth, who was bestowed upon me by Aśanivega.

Then the Teacher said: "For the sake of women whose minds are fickle..."
O Blessed One, what man with eyes could possibly take himself away from women, whose minds are as fickle as banners tossed by the wind? (SurSūCa.149)

He who is negligent regarding the Dharma is a base man, not a noble man. Furthermore, women, though filled with internal poison and possessing charming forms, are by their very nature like *guñjā* berries in their outward appearance. (SurSūCa 150–151)
Devoid of truth, compassion, and shame, these women are the source of evil deeds, rich in recklessness, and generators of fear; who with ears would find delight in them?
When passionate, they steal wealth; likewise, when dispassionate, they even steal life.

Whether in passion or even in dispassion, wicked young women are terrifying. They think of one thing in their minds, they act toward another, and they bestow [their favors] upon yet another; who indeed could be dear to those of such fickle hearts? (SurSūCa. 153–154)
They kill their own husbands for the sake of a lover;
alas! they place their trust in another and do not reveal their true nature.
(SurSūCa.155)

What is the use of saying more? Since they would kill even their own son, who indeed could be dear to such fickle women? Therefore, O blessed one, [be wary] of such women whose hearts are as flickering as flashes of lightning.
"Who here would be lax in their duty for the sake of women?
Having heard these words spoken by the Guru, Dhanavāhana laughed and said,
"Other young women indeed possess such wicked conduct."

But a great woman is upright, devoted to her husband, endowed with truthfulness, virtue, and compassion, affectionate, well-disciplined, firm in her love for her elders, and devoted to them. How could she be equal to other women of impure conduct? (SurSūCa.159)
"In this world, a great difference is seen between iron and horses.
Then the Guru said: "Even though that woman of yours is charming, nevertheless, when she is enjoyed, she is a path leading to the city of hell. (SurSūCa 160–161)

Just as the fruits of the *kimpāka* tree, when eaten, bring about suffering here in this world, so too does the pleasure of sexual union with women, though captivating to the mind, lead to a miserable rebirth. (SurSūCa.162)
Just as food mixed with poison, though delicious, takes away life when eaten, so too a beautiful woman, though enjoyed, surely bestows misfortune. Therefore,
abandon your passion for your own wife, who is the cause of an evil rebirth.
"May you become one endowed with the five great vows and devoted to right conduct.

(SurSūCa 164) Thus, being awakened day after day with words that inspire spiritual urgency and are sweet to the ear, he gradually developed a slight degree of affection [for the religious life]. (SurSūCa 165)

O soul!
O sinner! You shall wander for a long time among hell-beings and animals, your passion directed toward improper objects, even though you have obtained the faultless Dharma. (SurSūCa. 183–184)

In this manner, time passed for those two, who were devoted to the practice of self-restraint, austerity, and discipline, and intent on carrying out the commands of their teacher. Then, on a certain occasion, they were joined by their sister Vasumati.

there she saw a certain man accompanied by a woman, who was mad,
grey with dust and dirt, and clad in tattered rags.
Singing loudly and dancing much, surrounded by a troop of children, that wicked Maṇangavaī gazed for a long time at that pair.

In the inner apartments, she who was the foremost of all women in her entire harem became his beloved, for his heart was captivated by her exceedingly great passion. All this indeed happened while I was living with my father-in-law, right before my very eyes.

'This man appears seized by a spirit, looking exactly like the prince; therefore, this must surely be Kanakaratha, and she too is Sulocanā. (SurSūCa.194–195)
Anaṅgavatī said: "Let us converse with this sister of ours;

"What has happened, Blessed One? How has she become mad?
Then the Guru, having understood the reality through his knowledge, said: "She is indeed Sulocanā; this is Prince Kanakaratha."
The delusion of mind was cast upon their heads by one co-wife, who was overcome with jealousy;
through her influence, a confusion of mind arose for both of them. (SurSūCa.201)
Then the king summoned many experts in the sciences there;
yet none of them could ever restore them, for these [jewels] had somehow been carried away by the guards who were overcome by negligence over time.
And Vasumatī said: "O Blessed One, if you wish to show favor to these deluded-minded ones, please consider and grant them a remedy. (SurSūCa.204)
Then the teacher gave them a remedy established for destroying madness, and both sisters became restored to their natural state of mind.
Seeing the pair of sisters, Sulocanā was amazed and said this:
"What indeed is this dream, or is it a delusion of my mind?

"Both have taken their vows; where indeed are my two sisters here?

As long as the greatness of the Guru has not vanished, your infatuation will remain. And when you, O blessed one, were hungry in the inner apartments as the crown prince—*SurSūCa.209 [p.

thereafter,
I was awakened by the god Dhanavati-deva and became an ascetic at the feet of Candrayaśas.
This Anaṅgavatī also, having heard the Dharma and being terrified of the cycle of existence, took up the life of a renunciant here in this community together with her husband.
Therefore, O gentle one, what you have seen is not a dream; it is indeed the truth.
"This is that very same great being, our teacher named Sudharman.
Then both people, with supreme reverence, paid homage to the lotus-feet of the venerable Sudharman, which remove all faults.

Then, accompanied by her two sisters, Sulocanā— devoted to self-restraint and reverence for her guru—

"Indeed, many days have passed for all three sisters.

having remembered their former enmity, the wicked Aggikumāra-sura, who was like a bandhujīva flower, inflicted most terrifying calamities upon her. (SurSūCa.225–226)
That ascetic Kaṇagaraha, enduring that assault with right disposition together with the noble lady Sulōyaṇā, [attained liberation].
(SurSuCa.227 [p. 335])
Having passed away, both of them were reborn in the Candrārcis celestial mansion in the second kalpa as gods in the status of Sāmānika deities. (SurSūCa.

as they all experienced divine bliss together in that single mansion, their mutual affection for one another became exceedingly great.

that god Vijjuṣpaḥ, having fallen from that state, will [be born] here in this Vaitāḍhya range,

To Khayara, the one of immortal gait, was born from the womb of his beloved wife Cittamālā a dear daughter named Kaṇagamālā.

"Even though you practiced asceticism, because you did not abandon the state of passion,
as its fruit this unbearable calamity has befallen you.
In a former birth as a god, there was one who was your friend, named Candajjuṇa."
Having departed from there, he too was born here as Cittagati.
O Bhadra! The queen named Vasumati and Devī Candraprabhā were also born here in this world as Piyaṅgumañjarī in the celestial realm. (SurSūCa.242–243)

"O handsome one, because of that former association, a mutual and profound affection has arisen between you and Cittagati—even through their constant sight. Therefore, by means of a stratagem, she was united with you by Kaṇagamālā. (SurSūCa. 244)
Now, by the power of your own karma, this separation from her has come upon you.
O Cittavega! What is the use of saying more here? What else need be said?
I shall now explain to you exactly what was asked. That ascetic Kanakaratha was your own dear friend in a previous birth; from there, he became the god named Vihuprabha in the celestial realm.

This concludes the eighth excellent chapter, titled "The Description of Long-Acquainted [Friends]," in the *Surasundarī-kathā*, which serves as a water-mantra for quelling the fire of passion and the poison of hatred. (SurSuCa.249–250)

Today I have been commanded by the god Śaśiprabha:
"Go, Vihuppatha! Quickly, to the land of Bharata in Jambūdvīpa, to the city named Kuśagra, to the presence of the eminent sage Dhanavāhana. (SurSūCa.2–3)
He will see you there, established in meditation, by his former enemy;
seeing you, he will become enraged and inflict a most grievous assault.
Therefore, go quickly to that city for the sake of protecting him.
"I too shall return after having carried out Indra's command.
Having said "So be it," I have come here with speed.
Then, as he was fleeing accompanied by his beloved, you were seen by me.
Through my clairvoyant knowledge (*avadhijñāna*), I knew that this was indeed my friend Vidyutprabha, fleeing in haste, distressed by the fear of Nabhovāhana. (SurSūCa 6–7)
"This Nabhovāhana too has arrived here, clinging to this [chariot].

At that time, a divine jewel was handed over for the protection of the living being.

"O most wicked one! Causing pain to the sages who regard enemies and friends with equanimity, where are you going? You have fallen into the path of my vision!
When I had spoken thus, that god, a lord of the celestial palaces, became greatly agitated.
Immediately upon the monk’s entry into the dry meditation (śukladhyāna), his delusion vanished; thus, supreme, excellent, absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna) arose.

Hearing that sound of the drum, many gods and humans arrived; the Kevalin preached the Dharma to them, which is the cause of the bliss of liberation. (SurSūCa.15)

being evil-minded, is intent on taking away his life?"
The sage said: "Listen, how there was enmity in another birth.
In Dhātakīkhaṇḍa-Videha, there was an excellent city named Campā."
In that city, King Padma and the crown prince Samaraketu—

both of whom had their souls permeated by the words of the Jina and were bound together by brotherly affection— protected the kingdom and the burden of sovereignty according to the law of righteousness while observing partial renunciation.
When they had gathered in the assembly hall, the heretic Kapila arrived and declared:
"There is no soul, there is no omniscient one, and there is no liberation.
He was defeated in debate by the crown prince, who was well-versed in the meaning of the scriptures of the Jina’s doctrine.
When the crown prince was unable to give any reply, despite a multitude of arguments consisting of various logical reasons and illustrations,
he was then ridiculed by the chief ministers, high officials, and feudal lords.
He became utterly dejected and deeply distressed by Samaraketu, thinking:

(SurSūCa.25) "Therefore, having gone to his palace at night with sword in hand, I shall cut off his head, so that my mind may attain peace. (SurSūCa.26)
Having thus reflected while absorbed in the meditation of cruelty (rōddajjhāṇa),
he took up his weapons at night and entered the mountain cave of Samaraketu. Hidden by the fear of the horse-herdsman, he remained there, concealed.

"He is surely that Kapila, the nihilist (nāstikavādin) who was defeated by me in debate;
for the sake of his execution, he has entered here in disguise.
Having seen that Kapila with a dejected face and a trembling body, [the king spoke].
Compassion arose in the prince for one whose life was abandoned.
Then the prince said: "As long as you are still alive, you are released; having left my country, you must stay away, O wicked one!"
Thus addressed, he fled and went to a distant region,

"While this man is still alive, there is nothing for me that would bring satisfaction. (SurSūCa.46) When night had fallen, after performing his recitation (*svādhyāya*), the mendicants went to sleep; then, at midnight, Kapila arrived with the intent of killing the mendicants. (SurSūCa.47)

In a celestial mansion crowded with throngs of Apsarases, abundant happiness arose.

"O Bhadra! O Vihupphaha! That god who is now the lord of the celestial chariot is yours; by his command you have come into my presence. (SurSūCa.54)

"O Bhadda! O Vihuppaha! It was I who, while wandering, arrived here in this city today;

Having lived out an even longer lifespan than Sāgaramēgha,
he passed away and was reborn in the region of Magadha as a cowherd named Sābhaḍa;
having performed ascetic penance in his youth, he became a lord of the Bhavanavāsin gods.
The supreme deity of the Dharma named Uparuddha was born there;
seeing me come here, he has arrived in a great rage. Remembering that enmity, he has come for the purpose of slaying me.
Thus, O Vairanimitta, I have briefly explained this to you.
Then, O Cittavega, that Kevalin was asked by me once more: "Blessed One, what will be the duration of my life, and where will my rebirth take place? (SurSūCa. 64–65)
"Who will be dear to me, and who will awaken me to the religion of the Lord of Jinas?

then, at the exhaustion of that life, having passed away from there, you [will be born] in Hastināpura in the womb of Queen Kamalāvatī,

yet,
together with your mother, you will be carried off by a former enemy deity.
"O Cittavega! You shall prosper in the house of the Lord of the Sky-dwellers.

Having obtained the lay dharma from the teacher Supratiṣṭha, and then having attained the state of a śramaṇa, you will bring about the end of saṃsāra. (SurSūCa.
When this was spoken by the Kevalin, I honored his words, saying "So be it," circumambulated him, and again paid homage to that Blessed One.
Then, having flown up, he has arrived here in your presence.

how is she now? Is she still alive or not?

seeing her in that state, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose there.

No merit whatsoever accrued to that foolish woman who had swallowed the poison;

that young woman was carried by Nabhavahana’s retinue to the cremation ground;

that god who was previously hostile surely sports in this form.
