"Go back to your own place; your cleverness has been seen.
Thus mocked, she departed from there in anger with quivering lips.
And I too remained there happily, accompanied by my own people.
[In a pair of verses: On that very day, the king arrived at my mother’s house and was asked by her: "Why do you appear so full of anxiety? (SurSūCa. 70)
Then she said: "O Queen, you have indeed understood it correctly;
listen as I explain the cause of my great anxiety here.
[SurSūCa.71, p. 477]

The female ascetic named Vuddhilā, who had previously conquered Surasundarī in debate, took that painting of Surasundarī’s form which she had formerly painted upon her back while lost in thought. (SurSūCa. 72) Having taken that [painting] from her...
They arrived at Ujjain in the presence of King Sattuñjaya. Having shown him that [object], she of the wicked heart spoke to the king.
"O best of men! We wander the earth for your sake. Whatever jewel we see upon the earth, that we shall bring to you. This jewel among maidens was seen by me in the city of Kusagga. (SurSūCa.74–75)
"O King, who would be able to paint the body and form of this maiden Surasundarī, the daughter of King Naravāhaṇa, in its entirety? (SurSūCa.
76) And furthermore:
The Creator alone is that elder by whom this world was fashioned; otherwise, why would he not have made his own wife a treasury of happiness? (SurSūCa.77) [p.
Having fashioned her with such charming beauty, youth, and loveliness, Brahmā must surely have felt great pride in himself;
for she is capable of piercing the heart of even Love, who is already exhausted by the drawing of his bow. (SurSūCa 78)
"Truly, she has been fashioned by Fate like a hand-held spear.
Furthermore, whatever man shall take her hand in marriage, he will become a sovereign of half the land of Bharata; of this there is no doubt."
"O King! Thus it was declared by those possessing extraordinary knowledge regarding the time of her birth:
'That maiden is worthy of you, but not of anyone else. Then, having given much wealth with a joyful countenance, that king—
She said, "O Blessed One! It is reported that the maiden has been shown; you have acted well.
And this, O beautiful one, has all been told to me by my spies:
that Ratnacūḍa has been dispatched by him to my presence. (SurSūCa. 82–83)
Then his own minister by name approached me and requested:
"Let the maiden Surasundarī be given to King Sattuñjaya. (SurSuCa.84)
And I said this to him, based on the words of the fortune-teller Sumati: "O noble one!
He shall become the husband of the Vidyādhara maiden; therefore, she must be given by him to that very man. [SurSūCa.85]
"Food, for that elder is your master; so what need have you for his daughter?
Thereupon he replied, "Do not speak thus, O Lord of Men!
I have been sent by him with great respect; give me your own daughter."
"O Īti, by not giving [your daughter], I do not see anything good for you.
Then, being deeply incensed, I spoke thus: "I will not give my daughter; do whatever you please. (SurSūCa 87–88)
Therefore, go and report these words exactly as they occurred to your own master when he has returned home; moreover, what punishment can now be inflicted upon you? (SurSūCa.89) [p.
Then, having been informed that he had gone there, that proud man from Ujjayinī set out against us with his own army for the sake of battle.
Furthermore:

Surrounded by a multitude of foot-soldiers and chariots belonging to many kings and lords of men, he was accompanied by hundreds of thousands of camels whose hooves had pulverized the surface of the earth with their impact. (SurSūCa.
91) With the loud neighing of proud and fierce enemy elephants that struck terror into the ranks...
Accompanied by many great elephants as heavy as mountains,
that King Śatruñjaya— filled with intense rage and joined by a vast army—
arrived in our country, as reported by the spies. (SurSūCa 92–93)
[With three verses, a distinguishing feature:
"O Queen! Because of this omen, I have become filled with anxiety.
Then my mother said: "My beloved! Why worry about this? (SurSūCa. 94)
Having said, "O beautiful one," Kanakāvalī’s daughter Mayalekhā was given; thus he, having been honored, departed for his own abode. (SurSūCa.95) [p.
"Otherwise, he, possessing a vast army, will bring great calamity upon our weak country.
When this was said by the king, the minister replied:
"O Queen, this very thing was deliberated upon by the ministers; however, it was [only] the minister's [thought]."
This mantra conceived by Maṇisāgara was not auspicious:
"Since he said this, let him come here to Kusāgrapura; for his death has been foretold to me by a good dream. (SurSūCa 97–98)
And as that king was departing, there were ill-omened birds,
all bringing misfortune, and the planets, including Saturn, were extremely unfavorable. When he arrived here, victory was ours and defeat was his.
Therefore, O King, remain free from anxiety; what is the use of another person?
Let the construction of a bridge be undertaken, and let the village on that path be evacuated immediately; let them abandon their grass and fodder.
"Let wells be dug, let ponds and lakes be constructed, and let us go there with our forces for the purpose of preventing the enemy's passage. [SurSūCa.102]
"O Queen! Having carried out all the words of the minister, I have come here;
nevertheless, because of the power of the enemy, I have become filled with anxiety. Then, O female swan! however many days passed there in happiness...
On that very day, the city was besieged by the enemy army.
Then the gates were closed, the moats were filled with water,
and the warriors stood at the head of their ranks, equipped with armor and bound for battle.
Living beings are being slaughtered, various weapons are being sharpened,
and likewise the honoring of warriors is being performed; and every day,
rations are given as they advance toward the enemy army.
Brave warriors, elephants, horses, and excellent men fall on both sides;
the vassal lords are filled with doubt, and the citizens have become deeply distressed.
What indeed has become of our ministers, who were once undeluded regarding their duty?
Terrified cowards have fled from the onset of battle, while the warriors, whose wealth is their courage, are being steadied by the words of Sumati.
Thus it was, O Haṃsinī! When the city was in turmoil on all sides, one day I was sleeping upon the terrace of my bedchamber.
During the night, having seen myself being carried away by someone...
Awakened and terrified, she began to lament thus:
"Alas, mother! Alas, father! Some god or perhaps a celestial being is carrying me away!
Run, run, you warriors! Release me from this!"
While she was lamenting in this way, he said to her: "O gentle one, do not fear; I shall do nothing unpleasant to you, for you are as dear to me as my own life. (SurSūCa.113) [p.
"O beautiful one, why do you speak thus, terrified, when you have been carried off by me who am overcome by a heavy passion born from the sight of your form? O gentle lady,
I am a sky-dweller (khacara) residing on Mount Veyaddha, known as Mayarakeu."
"You shall enjoy pleasures with me; why do you weep, so distressed?
Having heard these words of his, I was delighted in my heart: "Could this truly be my husband, that Makarakaetu? (SurSūCa.115–116)
Even his wife, who was so affectionate and spoke so sweetly, having seen his form transformed by magic, became subject to the power of passion or went mad;
if even she is still practicing spells today, how indeed can there be any scripture for him?
"How am I so meritorious that he might be seen before my very eyes?"—
thinking thus, I was led by him to a certain place and set down upon the ground within a grove of plantain trees. (SurSūCa.118–119)
In the meantime, the night came to an end as if to correctly explain the ultimate truth:
"O child, look well! He is not that beloved; this is he. (SurSūCa.120)
When he was seen by Śyāmala at the time of dawn with his body restored, she then thought out of deep sorrow: "Alas! This is not him.
He was like pure gold in complexion and resembled the form of Ananga (the god of love) in beauty.

"In my mind, there is not even the slightest thing that resembles him. Therefore, what shall I do now? Deprived of refuge and under the power of another," as she was thinking thus, trembling arose within her out of fear. (SurSūCa.122–123)
Then, seeing me—my cheeks drenched by a spray of tears, trembling and terrified—he began to speak thus:
"O gentle lady, why are you afraid? You are [only] suspicious of ghosts and demons; fear not of me."
Listen, O gazelle-eyed one, as to who I am and for what purpose I have been carried away!
In the Veyaddha mountains there is a famous and excellent city called Gaṅgāvatta.
There, the king was the famous Śrīgandhavāhana. By Queen Madanāvalī, he had a second son named Nahavāhana, and a third, Mēghanāda, who was also known as Makaraka.
Nahavāhana, having mastered the sciences, then attained youth;
and for his sake, a noble maiden named Kaṇagamālā was chosen as his bride. At the time of the wedding, however, by one named Vijjāhara-Cittavega—
Having abducted her and married her, he became enraged at him; then,
having followed after him, he was bound by the Nāginī through her vidyā,
and taking Kaṇagamālā, he returned to his own city.
Then Vijjācchēda was born to Nahavāhana, by whom this [son] was born to the Vidyādhara who was accompanied by his wife. (Surūpa-sundarī-carita 131) [p.
The spells bestowed by his long-accustomed deity upon the sky-farer Cittavega enabled him to become a universal emperor (cakravartin) of the Vidyādharas; indeed,
all the lords of the sky-dwellers themselves came to pay him homage.
Having understood this, my father, filled with agitation, began to say:
"Behold, O sirs! The desires of men come to fruition in one way, yet by the power of destiny they turn out quite otherwise; indeed, the outcome of undertakings is different."
"Having made a firm resolve to become a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas,
you will fulfill your duty and take up the ascetic life in the presence of the Knower of the Absolute (Kevalin). But since that has turned out otherwise, what is the use of this kingdom?"
For the sake of Nārāyaṇa, we serve the pair of feet of the Protector. Victory! Indeed, cyclic existence is essence-less; and in hell, there is terrible and most cruel suffering! (SurSūCa.
136) jaō. saṁsārō hu asārō ghōrā aïdāruṇā ya narayammi!
The pains are difficult to endure; the transformation of karma is wondrous.
The range of the senses is fickle, and passion and hatred are difficult to conquer in the world.
The mind is unsteady, and sense objects are like the *kimpāka* fruit.
The separation from loved ones is exceedingly difficult to bear; women, who are as fickle as a lotus and whose speech is bitter with dispute, lead one toward the city of hell when they are indulged.
Life is as flickering as water stirred by the wind or a blade of kusa grass;
for all beings in this cycle of existence, death is certain.
Living beings are prone to deception, and the world is scorched by the wicked passions (kaṣāyas).

Household life has unpleasant results, and likewise, human birth is not easily obtained. (SurSūCa.141) An inclination toward the Dharma is rare; day and night one is beset by many obstacles; fortune is inherently fickle; and affection in this world is like a dream. (SurSūCa.142)
The fields of the noble ones are very difficult to find, and prosperity in the world of living beings is exceedingly rare;
yet, deluded by false views, living beings remain in a state of most terrible ignorance.
(SurSūCa.143)
As things decline, the states of existence (dharmas) become blameworthy;
one suffers from negligence, physical strength wanes, and even the lifespan becomes short.
What more need be said? (SurSūCa.144)
Since there is no refuge other than the Jina-dharma for living beings tormented by heavy and unbearable suffering in the realms of hell-beings,
animals, humans, and gods, I shall therefore go into the presence of the Father [the Teacher] and make this human birth fruitful.
Nahavāhaṇa said: "I too shall follow my father; for even one who carries out his commands has performed the duty of lordship. (SurSūCa.
146) Since...
having exercised sovereignty, [even] for one who executes the orders...
"What service shall we now perform for our own servant?
Then the father said, "This must be done by those endowed with discernment.
Thereupon, accompanied by his son, he performed what was appropriate for that occasion. (SurSūCa.147–148)
Having taken refuge at the feet of the Kevalin Suravāhana and having practiced stainless conduct,
he destroyed the eight karmas and became an Antagaḍa Kevalin.
(SurSūCa.149) [A yugma].
490] Then, by Cittavega, the lord of the Vidyādharas, I was consecrated as the king of the Vidyādharas right there in my own city, having been granted the entire region of my domain. (SurSūCa. 150)
While things were thus situated, for some reason, at the time of dawn, I set out alone from my own city for the Jewel Island (Ratnadvīpa).
O beautiful one! As I was traveling through the sky, I saw you sleeping upon the terrace of the palace.
"She has been carried off by me from the Maitālaka lake.
"Therefore, do not weep, O beautiful one! You are the mistress even of my life;
you shall enjoy pleasures with me upon the Veyaddha mountain."

Hearing those words, as if struck by a thunderbolt, she, being in great distress, began to think: "Alas, alas! On account of my own expansion of evil, my father has been attacked by that great enemy. (SurSūCa.
154) Thus she reflected.
I too have been carried away by him; though my heart was bound elsewhere, alas! fie! O friend!
by my very life, there is neither the father’s consolation nor the gain of a beloved.
"May he be happy as long as he lives, even though he has given [alms] to an enemy;
or rather, may I be happy by obtaining that which is dear to his heart. Yet, due to the ripening of my own evil karma, not even one of these things has come to pass. (SurSūCa.156–157)
While I was reflecting thus, I was addressed by him:
"Stay right here until I have gone to the nearby bamboo grove and, having returned, quickly give [it] to you by means of the *pannatti* spell. (SurSuCa.158)
"By means of preliminary service for a thousand births," having spoken thus,
he departed; I too remained there, tormented by grief for my teacher.

"What should be done? Deprived of refuge, terrified with fear, like a doe strayed from the herd, I remain weeping, my eyes filled with tears, casting anxious glances in all directions. (SurSūCa.160–161)
And then I saw nearby there a grove, beautiful with its wide-spreading *sāla* trees,
crowded with guñjā shrubs bent low by the weight of fruit trembling in the wind. (SurSūCa.162)
The mango grove possesses fruit that captivates the mind, spreading fragrance, and casting deep shade from its thick foliage;
it resounds with the cries of swarms of creatures falling while devouring its fruit, and the surface of the earth is filled with intoxicated birds that fall and flutter incessantly. (SurSūCa. 163)

Having seen that tree of death— which is lofty, which destroys the continuum of living beings, and which is like a poisonous tree— [I am] tormented by heavy suffering. (SurSūCa 164, in five stanzas) Having reflected upon it...

"O dear friends! O Haṃsinī! At that time, with my mind fixed on death, what shall I, wretched as I am, do while still alive—deprived of my beloved kinsmen and parents, and mocked by fate? Thus she reflected.
"Taking a fruit and placing it in my mouth as I go to his presence, may I not suffer such a mockery even in another birth. (SurSūCa.167) [p.
Having spoken thus with sorrow, while I remained there for a moment, she fell to the ground, overwhelmed by the intense pain of the poison. [SurSūCa.168;
a Kulaka consisting of three verses]
Then, O Bhadra, having reached a state that was indescribable, he was as if whirled around by the forest trees, as if uprooted from the entire earth,
as if his joints had fallen apart, and as if he were sinking down with all his limbs.
(SurSūCa.169)
I know nothing at all beyond this: that which has arisen for me is simply [the sight] of someone’s young son, who is like nectar,
as he gives him a jewel-water capable of quenching poison.

For just a moment, while he was sprinkling my body and personally massaging my limbs with his tender hands, she held a water-sprinkled palm-leaf fan in her hand and created a cool breeze. (SurSūCa.172)
My dear friend Priyaṃvadā has related to me my entire history, seen after so long a time, beginning from the viewing of the portrait and ending with that very event. (SurSūCa.173 [p. 494])

O Haṃsī, at that time, as he was listening for a moment with his limbs bristling with joy, she beheld herself; her painful sensations from the poison vanished, and she became comforted, thinking it was but a dream, and then she awoke. (SurSūCa. 174–175)
[In five stanzas: Then, opening my pair of eyes, I beheld a young man who resembled the God of Love, as if he had emerged from my own great heart, captivating the mind. (SurSūCa.176)

Seeing that, I thought: "What could this be? Is it a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), or perhaps another birth, or is it a dream? Or is it a delusion of my mind, or indeed is it actually real? (SurSūCa 177)
Or rather, no, no!
How could I have such merit that this person, so dear to my heart, might be seen with these very eyes?
And as for his being in her lap—where could such a thing possibly happen?
While she was reflecting thus, Priyamvadā addressed her:
"O Surasundarī! Why do you still look with a face upturned as if in wonder? (SurSūCa.180)
"This indeed is the Jewel Island, and this is my sister Piyaṃvayā; I am one who has mastered the sciences, and this is my brother Mayarakeu.
When she had spoken thus, she was delighted in her heart, thinking, "It is he indeed. (SurSūCa. 181)
With her body trembling from fear, she reached the space between the two [princes] who were closely pressed together.

In the meantime, a certain sky-goer (gandharva) arrived and, having shown humility, said:
"O Prince, the time for the worship of the Jina is approaching; arise!
Having heard those words, he placed Piyaṃvayā by my side.
Accompanied by only a few men, he reached the temple of the Jina.
Then, Piyaṃvayā asked him: "O dear one, how did you come here? [SurSūCa.185, p. 496]

"Why did you, having consumed poison, fall into such a terrible calamity on this jewel-island so difficult for mortals to traverse upon the earth? Then she related everything that had been said by me previously.
Then she too, having been questioned by me and having handed over the portrait to us,
where did she go at that time, and what did you do?
And how was I found in the terrifying forest, having consumed poison?
"How else could even a potent poison be removed from the body in an instant?
Piyaṃvada replied, "Having given you this picture-scroll,
I arrived here at this island of excellent jewels with great speed."
And having seen Makarakeu accompanied by his kinsmen and retinue, I remained here for several days out of affection for my sister. (SurSūCa.191) [p.
"O daughter! Having arrived here, I said: 'Stay right here;
remain as an attendant to Mayarakeu for now.
Then, saying 'So be it,' she remained on this island."

O gentle one! Standing near her husband, who was intent on mastering the sciences (*vidyā*), she learned that he had achieved success in the sciences and, accompanied by many kinds of celestial beings, had arrived here on this island for the sake of the eight-day festival (*aṣṭāhnikā*). // SurSuCa.193–194 //

Having performed the great festival for the glorification of the Lord of Jinas with magnificent splendor, having worshipped the vidyās according to the prescribed rule, and having honored those worthy of honor; having satisfied those worthy of worship and having bestowed gifts upon the realm of the sky-dwellers— SurSuCa.195.
Having celebrated the eight-day festival accompanied by dancing, singing, and instrumental music,
Māraketu also remained here this very day at the end of the night, having acquired a heap of jewels and performed his remaining duties.
[With three verses—*viśeṣaka*] [p.
Having performed the duties of the dawn, today I have gone out for the sake of attending to the body.
Near the bamboo thicket, he saw a polished sword;
out of curiosity, he seized that blade which resembled the tongue of Yama, possessing the luster of young *tamāla* leaves and a shimmering edge as beautiful as the moon. (SurSūCa 198–199)
In a nearby thicket, a clever spy suddenly struck a single blow and cut through that bamboo fence. (SurSūCa.200,
a yugma)
Then [he saw] one whose left hand was occupied with winding a thick string of pearls, whose eyes were fixed on his nose as he suppressed his breath through the practice of *vidyā*,
and who was intent upon perfecting that *vidyā* while seated in its midst. *SurSūCa.* 201.1–2.

Suddenly seeing the head of a certain Vidyādhara—its cheeks adorned with jeweled earrings—falling upon the earth, [the king], overcome with alarm, looked closely and cried out, "Alas! What is this? (SurSūCa.202–203)
And as he was observing closely,
he recognized:
"This is that one named Makarakeu."
"O Lord!
How is it that the noble son of King Gandhavāhana, Avvō, was killed by you while he was innocent and under the sway of negligence?
Alas! Alas! Fie upon ignorance for having committed this fruitless evil deed! (SurSūCa.204–205)

Thinking thus again and again and reproaching himself, as he had traveled only a short distance, his right eye throbbed. He thought, "I wonder if this auspicious omen portends something for me? *Sūtrakṛtāṅga-sūtra Commentary*, 206.

O fair one! Having seen you at the foot of the *visara* tree—your every limb enchanting, like the crescent moon, and a delight to the hearts of people—the prince was as if sprinkled with nectar upon beholding you, O beautiful lady! // SurSuCa.207-208 //
Oh, how is it that even this young woman, at the onset of her fresh youth, bestows such joy upon my heart as a beloved mistress does? (SurSūCa.209) [p.
"Is this [poison] of my own making, or has it been prepared by another?"— as she examined it,
she recognized it by means of the fragments of the poison-paste resting upon your face: "Alas,
this young girl has become unconscious due to the extremely intense transformation of the poison."
"Having brought her back, I shall restore her to her own place through this medical treatment.
O Surasundarī! Having thought thus and taken you, the merchant arrived here and related to me the entire account as previously described. (SurSūCa.211–212)
And I was told by him: "Wash this ring quickly;
it was given by my father at the time of bestowing the vidyās, adorned with a divine gem, and is a warder-off of the spread of all evils. (SurSūCa.213)
Furthermore, having obtained the necessary conditions, especially regarding the collection of poisons,
the Khecarakumāras were told: "Quickly prepare the materials for the worship."
Having brought this [image] here and performed the worship of the Jina,
I shall perform the rite of propitiation (*santikarma*) for the sake of overcoming obstacles and the recitation of mantras.
Desiring the purification of the sin incurred by the abduction of the Vidyādhara woman,
in the meantime, I gave him this ring. (SurSūCa.216 [a pair])
O gentle one! By this method of drinking water, you have been restored to health.
O beautiful lady! While I am yet to relate before him the account of the vision in the painted panel, you have regained consciousness.
"All that you asked has been explained by me;
therefore, O Surasundarī, everything you desired is accomplished.
Or rather: [SurSuCa.219] ahavā.
"Even from across the ocean, from the midst of the sea, or from a distant land, a favorable destiny brings together what is desired," so it is said.
Then I replied: "It is indeed so; however, listen."
Because of me, my father remains afflicted by powerful enemies;
even though Priyadarśanā has been born, my heart is still deeply overwhelmed with grief. (SurSūCa.221)
"O friends! My torment still afflicts my body.
Śatruñjaya has begun [his ritual] and the lives of living beings are in danger;
therefore, how can there be favor from Fate for me, one of such meager fortune? (SurSūCa.222–223)
Having spoken thus, O female swan, she began to weep from the force of her grief;
at that moment, her brother arrived, having performed his necessary duties.
He said to her: "O lady of lovely speech, why is your dear sister weeping?"
He explained all of that to her as the cause of his sorrow.
Then he said, "O beautiful one, do not weep;
I shall certainly go this very day and lead the enemy of your father before the mouth of Death."
"O beautiful one, while I am alive, who could possibly overcome your father?
Therefore, I shall go there now, accompanied by my arms.
[SurSūCa.227, p. 503]
Right here, in this first temple of the Jina, you should remain at your ease, free from sorrow, accompanied by Piyaṃvada,
until I return to slay the wicked-spirited enemy Jaya.
Having spoken thus, he flew up into the sky with the sword of Vasunanda in his hand.
Accompanied by Priyaṃvadā, I too remained right there that day,
full of great passion and thinking only of my reunion with him.
"Has my heart's beloved still not come quickly today, having suddenly slain that wicked man, even though he is empowered by the mastery of spells?

"Anxious as to why he has not yet returned, while I was still waiting,
there appeared one who was terrifying in his true form— reproaching me with harsh and cruel words, and formidable with a mass of matted hair tawny like the rows of smokeless flames of fire."

His appearance is terrifying; he is one who causes the heads of men to dance upon the tips of his hands; he is difficult to behold with eyes that are tawny like the hollows of desert wells. (SurSūCa.234)

Adorned with a garland of human skulls jingling with the sound *khalakhalakhaliṃta*, his long tongue flickered, bright as a mass of lightning; terrifying all throngs of living beings with the resonance of his formidable, loud laughter. (SurSūCa. 235)
A terrifying, hideous-faced *vetāla* arrived there.
[SurSuCa.236, in five stanzas] "O sinner! Since at that time, with your mind attached to another man, you..."

By that most wicked man, who was lustful for another's wife, great suffering was inflicted upon me; he has now obtained the fruit thereof. You too shall now receive the fruit corresponding to your own deeds; actions indeed bear fruit.
Speaking thus, O female swan, he seized me as I was trembling with fear and flew up into the sky, threatening me with harsh words. (SurSūCa.239) [Three verses in a *kulaka*]
[She] addressed with harsh words her beloved, who was following closely behind her path, suddenly making her feel as if her life had departed by uttering terrifying roars. (SurSūCa.240)
Having been cast from the sky by that wicked one to a distant land, with all his limbs crushed to pieces, he was surely killed with the intention that he should die. (SurSūCa.241,
a yugma)
By the power of destiny, she fell into that garden of creepers and was seen by Samantabhadra; he questioned her about the events, asking:
"Is this a magical illusion, or is it a dream? Or where have you come from?"
Where has the Vetāla gone, and what has happened to Piyaṃvada?
I suspect that some unpleasant thing must have been done by this [Vetāla] to Manavallabha;
for that reason, he has not yet returned to that island.
